AMC Theatres launched Leawood Films, a distribution label for fully financed, completed small and mid-budget movies, with first titles due in 2027 or 2028. Filmmakers keep ownership of their IP and downstream revenues. Advisors are former Warner Bros Group chairman Toby Emmerich, former Walt Disney Studios marketing president Ricky Strauss, and Kyle Davies, who leaves Bleecker Street. They report to AMC chairman and CEO Adam Aron.
Why This Matters
Aron framed the label around excess screen capacity rather than a content ambition, and the structure follows: Leawood takes no ownership. For a finished film with no distributor, that removes the usual price of access, which is rights. A service deal with retained ownership is now a live option, and offers on festival orphans get measured against it.
Specific Implication
Producers holding completed, unsold festival titles have a distributor to approach that does not ask for the IP. Test the marketing spend AMC commits, and how it guarantees bookings outside its own circuit.
The Facts
  • AMC Theatres announced Leawood Films on Monday, August 31, 2026, a distribution label for small and mid-sized movies that are fully financed and completed. AMC's release bills it as a "low-risk opportunity."
  • Filmmakers retain ownership of their feature IP and downstream revenues. Deadline describes Leawood as "a gun-for-hire distributor."
  • Variance handles North American booking and distribution; AMC oversees marketing; Piece of Magic Entertainment handles overseas distribution.
  • Windows: a 45-day exclusive theatrical window or greater before premium VOD, and a 90-day window to streaming.
  • The slate will be booked at rival circuits globally. First titles are to be announced for release in 2027 or 2028.
  • The label is named for Leawood, Kansas, where AMC is headquartered. Offices there and in Los Angeles.
  • Advisors: former Warner Bros Group chairman Toby Emmerich; former Walt Disney Studios marketing president Ricky Strauss; former Paramount distribution veteran Kyle Davies, who is exiting Bleecker Street for the venture. Entertainment attorney Craig Jacobson of Hansen Jacobson represents the label. All report to AMC Entertainment chairman and CEO Adam Aron.
  • Aron: "Leawood Films is being created with a straightforward objective, given that substantial excess capacity exists in the movie theatre industry: to bring more movies to theatres."
  • Aron: "This is a modestly scaled initiative focused on taking to the big-screen films that are fully financed by their filmmakers... It is highly unlikely that Leawood Films will include blockbuster tentpole-type releases. So, our Leawood Films effort is intended to complement, not compete with, the crucial work of our longstanding existing partnerships with major studios and key distribution partners."
  • Aron: "Through Leawood Films, we believe we can bring meaningful value to filmmakers whose movies might otherwise not get made, or which might not be taken to theatres. We can assure them the availability of movie theatre screens and attractive economics."
  • Variance previously handled AMC's own theatrical releases: Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour (2023, $180.7M domestic / $261.6M worldwide), Taylor Swift: The Official Release Party of a Showgirl (2025, $34M domestic opening weekend / $50M worldwide) and Renaissance: A Film by Beyonce ($33.8M domestic / $44M worldwide).

Paramount extended its Warner debt offers for the tenth time, to September 11
About 66 percent of the tender notes and 75 percent of the exchange notes are in hand, and holders can withdraw every one of them before the deadline.
CEO Summary
Paramount Skydance said Monday it has pushed the expiration of its tender and exchange offers for Warner Bros. Discovery notes to September 11. Tender and exchange offers are bids to buy back or swap a company's existing bonds. It is the tenth extension since June 12. Paramount said it expects to keep extending until settlement can occur at or just after the acquisition closes. As of August 28, roughly 66.28 percent of the tender notes and 75.48 percent of the exchange notes had been validly tendered.
Why This Matters
Paramount is carrying an open bond exchange it cannot close, because settlement is wired to a closing date the antitrust litigation controls. BofA Securities and Citigroup have kept the offers live since June on a rolling two-week leash. Every extension restores each holder's withdrawal right, so the 66.28 and 75.48 percent are a running poll of bondholder patience that resets rather than committed capital.
Specific Implication
Anyone pricing Warner paper against a near-term settlement is pricing a date Paramount has said in its own release it does not control.
The Facts
  • Paramount Skydance Corporation (NASDAQ: PSKY) announced on August 31, 2026 that the expiration dates for its previously announced tender offers and exchange offers have been extended to 5:00 p.m. New York City time on September 11, 2026, unless further extended.
  • The offers cover notes issued by Discovery Global Holdings, Inc. (formerly WarnerMedia Holdings, Inc.) and Discovery Communications, LLC. Paramount is offering cash for the tender notes and newly issued Paramount notes for the exchange notes.
  • Prior extensions were announced on June 12, June 26, July 13, July 17, July 24, July 31, August 7, August 17 and August 24, 2026. The August 31 announcement is the tenth.
  • Paramount said it anticipates continuing to extend the expiration dates "until such time that would result in the Settlement Dates occurring on or promptly following the closing date of the proposed acquisition" of Warner Bros. Discovery.
  • As of 5:00 p.m. New York City time on August 28, 2026, approximately 66.28% of the aggregate principal amount of the Existing Tender Offer Notes and approximately 75.48% of the Existing Exchange Offer Notes had been validly tendered. Paramount said it does not view these figures as representative of final results.
  • Tenders may be withdrawn at any time prior to the expiration date.
  • Settlement is "currently anticipated to occur in the third quarter of 2026."
  • Notes eligible to participate include the DCL 3.950% senior notes due 2028 ($1,234,458,000, tender offer), 4.125% due 2029 ($655,825,000), 3.625% due 2030 ($914,183,000), 5.000% due 2037 ($453,281,000), 6.350% due 2040 ($438,102,000), 4.950% due 2042 ($130,366,000) and 4.875% due 2043 ($141,584,000).
  • BofA Securities and Citigroup are dealer managers. Global Bondholder Services Corporation is exchange agent and information agent.

The FTC and 22 states sued Amazon over ad auction prices, alleging more than $20 billion in overcharges
The complaint says Amazon began secretly manipulating auction results in 2018 using a hidden surcharge and artificial bids. Almost half of the 1.2 million affected advertisers were small or medium-sized businesses.
CEO Summary
The Federal Trade Commission and 22 state attorneys general sued Amazon on Monday in the Western District of Washington, alleging it deceived advertisers by inflating prices in its ad auctions. The complaint covers sponsored products, brands and display ads sold against retail search results. Amazon said it strongly disagrees, calling the suit misguided and saying the claim "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate."
Why This Matters
This is the FTC's third major suit against Amazon and the first aimed at how the ad auction itself sets a price.

Amazon's own defense concedes the mechanics are opaque to buyers. It argues advertisers "adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics," which is a claim that disclosure does not matter because outcomes discipline spend.

Emarketer's Zak Stambor told CNN that "Amazon is incredibly hard to walk away from." Advertisers who believe they were overcharged still have to keep buying while the case runs.
Specific Implication
Media buyers who have run Amazon campaigns since 2018 fall inside the group the complaint describes, and the restitution the FTC seeks would be calculated against auction records Amazon holds.
The Facts
  • The Federal Trade Commission and 22 state attorneys general sued Amazon on Monday, August 31, 2026, in U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington.
  • The complaint alleges Amazon "likely illegally extracted over 20 billion dollars" from 1.2 million advertising customers. Almost half were small or medium-sized businesses.
  • Alleged mechanism: "in 2018, Amazon began secretly manipulating its auction results to increase its ad prices," through a hidden surcharge and artificial bids.
  • Amazon's ad auction is second-price: the winning advertiser is supposed to pay one cent more than the second-place bid.
  • The suit covers sponsored products, sponsored brands and display advertisements sold against search results on Amazon's retail site.
  • The FTC and states allege violations of federal and state consumer protection statutes and seek civil penalties, restitution and additional relief.
  • The complaint says the higher costs were eventually passed down to Amazon shoppers.
  • Amazon's response, a roughly 3,000-word statement to CNN, says it "strongly disagrees" with the "misguided" lawsuit: "The FTC's claim fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate. Advertisers adjust bids based on real-world performance, not descriptions of auction mechanics."
  • Amazon added that even accepting the FTC's premise, it estimates advertisers "saved over $8 billion from 2021 to 2025 as a result of Amazon prioritizing ad relevancy over selecting ads on bid price alone." Amazon says it shared data with the FTC "on multiple occasions."
  • Amazon became the third-biggest ad platform in the United States in 2018.
  • Emarketer principal analyst Zak Stambor: "Advertisers face a tough challenge because Amazon is incredibly hard to walk away from." Emarketer puts Amazon's 2026 worldwide retail ecommerce sales at $927.82 billion.
  • University of Notre Dame marketing professor Vamsi Kanuri told CNN that auction-based ad buying "relies entirely on platforms strictly adhering to well-established rules."
  • Prior FTC matters: a $2.5 billion settlement last year over Prime enrollment practices ($1 billion civil penalty plus $1.5 billion in refunds to about 35 million customers), and a settlement of more than $30 million in 2023 over Alexa and Ring privacy claims. Amazon denied wrongdoing in both.
  • This is the FTC's third major lawsuit against Amazon.

Gal Gadot spent six months negotiating AI protections, and SAG-AFTRA asked her lawyers for pointers
Doug Liman shot Bitcoin's cast in a barebones warehouse. Producer Ryan Kavanaugh has claimed the $70 million production avoided more than $200 million in cost by generating its production design and lighting.
CEO Summary
Gal Gadot told the Happy Sad Confused podcast that her contract on Doug Liman's Bitcoin took six months to negotiate, the longest of her career, because her lawyers worked through every scenario involving the film's AI component. She said she required that AI not touch her performance, and that SAG-AFTRA called her lawyers for pointers on updating its own contract to protect other actors. AI use on the film covers sets and lighting.
Why This Matters
A union asking a member's lawyers how to write its own protections shows where the drafting is happening. The template for AI performance carve-outs is being set deal by deal, by the performers with leverage enough to fund that drafting, and backfilled into collective terms afterward. Everyone below that leverage line signs whatever language exists at the time.
Specific Implication
Gadot's contract draws the line at sets and lighting: AI may build them, and may not alter a performance. Ask for that boundary by name in any deal on a production using generative tools.
The Facts
  • Gal Gadot spoke on the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast with host Josh Horowitz, promoting her Prime Video action film The Runner. Variety published the account on August 31, 2026.
  • On Doug Liman's Bitcoin: "This was the longest contract I have ever worked on. It was six months from my lawyers to go through every scenario we could think about as far as the AI component of it."
  • "I did not want AI to have anything to do with my performance. We had to protect that, to such an extent that SAG called my lawyers to ask for pointers to update the SAG contract to protect other actors. As far as the performances, it's all me."
  • "I am afraid of AI, but I am going to be afraid and look away? No... The train has left the station. You're going to work with it or be out of the game completely. I am trying to make the best of it and protect what I can protect. The AI component in this movie is for sets and the lighting."
  • Bitcoin's cast, which includes Gadot, Casey Affleck, Pete Davidson and Isla Fisher, was shot in a completely barebones space.
  • Producer Ryan Kavanaugh has claimed the $70 million production saved more than $200 million by using AI to fill in production design and lighting.
  • Gadot on the shoot: "Here we would film nonstop because we didn't have to wait for lighting. We would film on and on and on for 10 hours." She compared the experience to theatre because only the actors were on set.
  • Separately in the same interview, Gadot said she would likely not return for a third Wonder Woman, citing her life with four children. On DC Studios' handling of the transition: "The Henry [Cavill] situation was not handled elegantly to say the least. Patty [Jenkins] was not handled elegantly. We're all adults and we're all good."
  • Wonder Woman (2017) grossed $824 million worldwide.

Agencies are signing Love Island contestants within days, and NBCUniversal holds them for a year first
Season 8 drew 19 billion minutes and 7.9 million views on Peacock. UTA signed winner Bryce Alakai a week after the finale, and Gersh represents host Ariana Madix and contestant Kenzie Annis.
CEO Summary
Variety reported Monday that leading agencies now treat Peacock's Love Island USA as a talent pipeline, with UTA, Gersh and WME all signing from recent seasons. Contestants leave the villa under a one-year exclusivity deal that limits what opportunities they can take, which the reporting says usually keeps them inside NBCUniversal. Peacock viewership doubled at Season 6 and has grown since.
Why This Matters
Attention on a contestant peaks at the finale and decays from there. A twelve-month hold captures that peak for NBCUniversal, and that window, more than the show itself, is what the format monetizes.

Gersh's Jade Sherman described the counterparty position directly: the franchise "tries really hard to protect their IP," and "it's on us as representatives to be able to pivot and adapt to where their changing rules are." Representation is being priced against terms the platform sets and revises.
Specific Implication
Agents weighing a reality-format signing should read the exclusivity term before the follower count. UTA's Jamie Youngentob said Bryce Alakai was attractive for a DJ career that predated the show, which is the asset the window does not cover.
The Facts
  • Season 8 of Love Island USA drew 19 billion minutes watched, translating to 7.9 million views, according to Peacock data cited by Variety.
  • Season 6 viewership doubled compared with previous seasons, according to NBCUniversal, and has grown in the two years since.
  • The Bravo-branded "Aftersun" spinoff, co-hosted by Summer House star Ciara Miller, saw a 135% viewership increase from last season. Other spinoffs include Beyond the Villa and Love Island Games.
  • The show is produced by ITV America and airs on Peacock. It launched on CBS in 2019 with Arielle Vandenberg hosting, moved to Peacock for Season 4 with Sarah Hyland, and Ariana Madix took over as host in Season 6.
  • Contestants leave under a one-year exclusivity deal that limits what opportunities they can take, which Variety reports usually means keeping them inside the NBCUniversal family.
  • UTA signed Season 8 winner Bryce Alakai just over a week after the finale aired, per UTA partner and agent Mahzad Babayan.
  • Gersh represents Emmy-nominated host Ariana Madix and Season 8 contestant Kenzie Annis.
  • Season 7 contestant Iris Kendall signed with WME and turned expected one-off brand deals into a full-time career.
  • UTA unscripted TV agent Jamie Youngentob: "I don't think we've seen anything quite like this. The closest thing would probably be Bravo, but those shows can take multiple seasons for somebody to really break through and stick."
  • Youngentob on why UTA signed Alakai: "He's been working incredibly hard at pursuing and building a DJ career. That was exciting for us, alongside our music colleagues." Alakai had a music career before the show and appeared in a Tubi film.
  • Gersh head of digital Jade Sherman: "Love Island is an incredible brand, and they try really hard to protect their IP. They've put things in place to do that, and it's on us as representatives to be able to pivot and adapt to where their changing rules are."
  • The show now connects departing Islanders with agencies and publicists, which Season 6 did not offer.
  • The finale prize is $100,000, voted on by viewers. The Season 8 reunion dropped August 31.
  • Season 6 contestant Kaylor Martin, a college senior with about 4,000 Instagram followers when she applied, is now a full-time content creator hosting her own podcast.

Summer box office stands at $4.598 billion with eight days left to beat 2013

CEO Summary
The North American box office from the first Friday in May through August 30 stands at $4.598 billion, according to Rentrak, the second-highest summer on record behind the $4.756 billion of 2013. Eight days of the season remain through Labor Day. Rentrak's Paul Dergarabedian said a like-for-like 123-day comparison would put summer 2026 at about $4.612 billion through August 31.
Why This Matters
Two titles carried a third of the season. Spider-Man: Brand New Day is about 20 percent of the summer on its own, and with The Odyssey the pair reach close to 32 percent.

That concentration is the useful number. A record-adjacent summer built on two tentpoles from Sony and Universal says the marginal dollar sits at the top of the slate, which argues for fewer and larger bets rather than a broader release calendar.
The Facts
  • Per Rentrak, the North American box office from the first Friday in May through end of day August 30 stands at $4.598 billion, the second-highest summer ever behind summer 2013's $4.756 billion.
  • The gap to the record is $158 million. Deadline reports that some sources estimate the season could come up $18 million to $22 million short.
  • The August 28-30 weekend did $100 million in the U.S. and Canada across all titles per Rentrak, up 46% over the same frame a year ago.
  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day took its fifth No. 1 weekend with $22.2 million.
  • Ketchup Entertainment's release of Warner Bros. Animation's Coyote vs. Acme opened to $15.4 million, the distributor's biggest opening ever, matching presales and tracking.
  • The only new major-studio wide entry next weekend is Paramount's Mark Wahlberg crime drama By Any Means. Spider-Man is forecast at $18 million to $20 million over the four-day holiday.
  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day is expected within days to become the second movie ever to cross $900 million domestic, after Star Wars: The Force Awakens, which stands at $936.66 million.
  • Spider-Man: Brand New Day, directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, represents around 20% of the entire summer's business. With Universal's The Odyssey, at $563.8 million and Christopher Nolan's highest-grossing film, the two account for close to 32% of all ticket sales from the first Friday of May through August 30.
  • Paul Dergarabedian, Rentrak's Head of Marketplace Trends: "No matter where the final number lands, we have to keep the calendar in mind. There are still eight days of box office to be added from Monday, August 31 through Labor Day Monday, Sept. 7, giving this year a full 130-day summer movie season. For a true apples-to-apples comparison, the first 123 days of Summer 2026 should be compared with the 123-day summer of 2013. Based on the current forecast, Summer 2026 should stand at approximately $4.612 billion through Monday, August 31, making it the second-highest-grossing 123-day summer movie season of all time."
  • Dergarabedian: "I don't think it really matters at this point whether we beat the record. This has been such a spectacular moviegoing season that the numbers are just that and the incredible mix of films presented to audiences this year has been a game changer, not only for the industry, but for younger moviegoers."

Markiplier bought 8.5 percent of GoPro and is now its largest shareholder
GoPro is worth about $110 million, has warned it may not survive twelve months, and its largest shareholder is a YouTuber who self-released a $51 million movie.
CEO Summary
Mark Fischbach, the YouTube creator known as Markiplier, has taken an 8.5 percent stake in GoPro, making him its largest single shareholder. GoPro is valued at roughly $110 million, its shares are down more than 90 percent over five years, and the company has said there is substantial doubt about its ability to continue as a going concern. Fischbach told Bloomberg the stock looked undervalued and that he wants the company to succeed.
Why This Matters
An 8.5 percent stake in a company valued near $110 million costs under $10 million, roughly three times what Iron Lung cost to make. Fischbach said the position sits alongside an investment in Strada and is meant to push his audience toward feature production. That makes it a supply-side bet. He is buying the tools his viewers would need before they need them.
Specific Implication
A camera vendor operating under a going-concern warning is a live counterparty risk for any production standardizing on its hardware.
The Facts
  • Mark Fischbach, the YouTube creator known as Markiplier, has acquired an 8.5% stake in GoPro, making him the largest single shareholder.
  • GoPro is valued at about $110 million. Its shares are down more than 55% this year and more than 90% over the past five years.
  • GoPro said in May it was exploring strategic alternatives and has since said there is "substantial doubt about the company's ability to continue as a going concern for the next twelve months."
  • Fischbach: "I saw the stock and where it was, I was like that seems undervalued. It's just something I've been cooking in the background; I want the company to succeed."
  • He has also invested in Strada, which makes tools for transferring large files between filmmakers.
  • Fischbach is 37, has posted as Markiplier for about 15 years, and has nearly 40 million YouTube subscribers.
  • His film Iron Lung grossed $51 million on a $3 million budget and was distributed by Fischbach himself, without a major studio.
  • He used GoPro cameras for behind-the-scenes footage on Iron Lung but did not consider them good enough for principal photography.
  • That changed when he saw a teaser for GoPro's Mission 1 Pro ILS, an interchangeable-lens camera weighing 6.95 ounces that the company calls a cinema camera.
  • Fischbach attended the National Association of Broadcasters trade show in Las Vegas in April to see GoPro's next camera.
  • Fischbach: "One of the things I want to do is push my audience to the risky world of trying to make feature films and higher-end productions."

Representatives working with creator-owned companies should expect packaging value to move from the show to the corporate transaction, because the format never reaches a licensing market.

Anna Gomez, the only Democrat on the Federal Communications Commission, told The Hollywood Reporter she wants to be renominated. Gomez can hold her seat into 2027 without another confirmation vote, and that carryover is the whole of her leverage. For a broadcaster with a renewal pending, that vote count is the operative fact.
Specific Implication
Companies holding broadcast licenses should price early-renewal risk into station and network valuations, since the agency has now tied a renewal review to a company's internal policies.
The Facts
  • Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner at the Federal Communications Commission, told The Hollywood Reporter: "I'd love to be reconfirmed, and I have supporters in the Senate, which I'm very grateful for, and appreciate very much." She added: "I think it's important that we maintain somebody that pushes back against this administration's overreaches."
  • Gomez's term ended at the end of June. She is in a carryover period that could last until the end of 2027 unless another commissioner is nominated and confirmed by the Senate before then.
  • The law caps commissioners from a single party at three. The commission is typically five members and can operate with a quorum of three.
  • Gomez was appointed under President Biden in 2023 and confirmed 55-43. Republican Brendan Carr chairs the agency; Republican Olivia Trusty was named a commissioner in 2025.
  • Earlier this month President Trump nominated Carr's senior counsel, Danielle Thumann, a Republican, for a five-year commissioner term. She has not been confirmed. The President has not said whether he would fill a fifth seat or support Gomez's renomination.
  • Gomez dissented from the FCC's 2-1 approval of the Paramount-Skydance merger, which required the company to eliminate its DEI programs and put controls on newsroom decisions at CBS.
  • Last spring she launched a nationwide First Amendment tour.
  • She has been outspoken on the FCC's decision to call Disney's broadcast licenses for early renewal, which the agency tied to Disney's DEI policies and which followed administration calls for action against Jimmy Kimmel over a joke.
  • Gomez, in a May social media post: "The FCC is once again targeting an administration critic by mob rule. Let's not pretend this FCC hasn't already made up its mind. All they want is for their pro-censorship partisan allies to nod in agreement. My message to Disney: Don't flinch. Fight."
  • Gomez said she hopes she "played no small part in ensuring that Disney did stand up and sue the FCC about this retaliation."
  • Carr previously said in a hearing that "any broadcaster that complies with the public interest standard is not in any risk at all," and, pressed on retaliation, that "there is no First Amendment right to an FCC license." He also said the FCC was "not formally an independent agency."
  • Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) told Punchbowl News in April: "It is not government's job to censor speech, and I do not believe the FCC should operate as the speech police."
  • Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA) and Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) support Gomez's renomination and a return to a five-member bipartisan commission.
  • Gomez says broadcasters ask her whether it is safe to report on given topics: "the fact that you're asking me that question is the problem because it is not for the FCC to make your editorial decisions."
  • She warns early license renewals "devalue the licenses themselves."

John Ternus, Apple's hardware chief, becomes chief executive on September 1, succeeding Tim Cook after 15 years. Cook began seriously considering him as a successor two years ago. Apple's revenue roughly quadrupled to $416 billion during Cook's tenure and its market value rose fifteenfold.

Apple TV+ reports into services, and services is the one line Apple's own executives told Bloomberg they expect to keep decelerating. They attribute the slowdown to weak game purchases as users move to TikTok, to App Store take rates lowered under regulatory pressure, and to the EU forcing Apple to admit independent app stores. None of those causes can be fixed with better shows.

Bloomberg also reports that the heads of marketing, services and retail have each been at Apple about four decades and could retire within a few years, and that roughly half the leadership team could exit. A content commitment underwritten by a relationship with Cue now carries a shorter sponsor horizon than the deal term.

Producers and representatives negotiating Apple TV+ commitments should expect approval to route through a division defending its own growth rate, and should check whether renewal or extension terms depend on a single executive relationship.

Phil Tippett has closed the Berkeley visual effects studio he ran for four decades, auctioning stop-motion models, cameras, fabrication equipment and production material. Specific Implication
Productions planning practical, stop-motion or motion-control sequences should book physical capacity at contracting rather than assume the vendor holds it in house.

The two publishers filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Catalog owners licensing to lyric and metadata services should check whether those agreements bar downstream AI ingestion. The complaint points at the licensee as the leak point.

Bake Off's Former Producers Are Suing Sky as It Closes Its £1.6 Billion ITV Takeover
Letty Kavanagh, Love Productions' former managing director, has filed two UK lawsuits against Sky and claims £755,752 in unpaid severance, nine months after being fired for objecting to Sky's attempt to move Bake Off behind its own paywall.
CEO Summary
Sky, owned by Comcast, bought Love Productions outright in 2020. In early 2025 Sky content chief Cecile Frot-Coutaz launched Project Rise, an effort to move The Great British Bake Off off Channel 4 and onto Sky. Love's executives objected. Sky abandoned the plan, renegotiated the Channel 4 renewal directly in October 2025, and fired Kavanagh in November. Sky has since installed new management at Love and agreed to sell the company to ITV Studios for £200 million as part of its ITV takeover.
Why This Matters
Kavanagh's central allegation is about price, not principle: she says the renewal Sky negotiated without her was "materially less advantageous" than the terms she had agreed with Channel 4 in 2024, costing millions of pounds across the contract and side deals including the Netflix licensing agreement in the US.

Sky answers that it owned Love and Bake Off outright and could do as it liked. Both positions are probably correct, which is the useful part. Full acquisition hands the buyer the right to decide while the relationship expertise stays with the people who built it, so a buyer acting entirely within its rights can still take value out of the asset it just paid for.
Specific Implication
Producers selling into a broadcaster group should price the customer relationship separately from the label, through earnouts tied to renewal terms rather than to output.
The Facts
  • Kavanagh spent 18 years at Love Productions and was fired in November 2025.
  • Two suits filed: an employment tribunal claim (wrongful dismissal, sex discrimination) and a High Court claim for £755,752 ($1 million) in severance.
  • Two others complained to Sky: former Bake Off executive producer Kieran Smith and a third unnamed person still employed by Love.
  • Project Rise ran January to November 2025; Sky abandoned it, reportedly after failing to convince judges including Paul Hollywood to switch.
  • Sky's plan would have dropped the professionals and kids' spin-offs.
  • Gibson Dunn investigated the whistleblowing complaints and did not substantiate them. Kavanagh and Smith dispute the rigour of that review.

California Carves Independent Film Out of Its New $5 Million Tax Credit Cap; Studios Get a Faster Cash Refund Instead
Independent film accounts for 10% of the $750 million program and gets the only full exemption. Studios instead get their cash refund in two years at a 5% discount, down from five years at 10%.
CEO Summary
California lawmakers unveiled AB 186 on Friday evening, a trailer bill amending the state's $750 million film and TV incentive after June's Senate Bill 122 capped the tax credits any business may claim at $5 million or 70% of liability per year. Independent productions are fully exempt from that cap. Major studio productions are not, and instead get a faster, cheaper cash refund on credits they elect to monetize. Both houses must pass the bill by midnight Monday, the last day of the legislative session.
Why This Matters
Sacramento refused the full carveout the Motion Picture Association and the Entertainment Union Coalition asked for, and the stated reason is the constraint worth remembering: a film-specific exemption would have brought tech asking for the same one, which would have hollowed out SB 122. That sets the terms for every future ask. Relief that arrives inside a general business-tax vehicle can pass. Relief framed as Hollywood's alone runs into an argument about who else is in line.
Specific Implication
Independent producers can again pledge an uncapped California credit to financiers. Studios should reprice their credits at a 5% discount received over two years before the next round of location decisions.
The Facts
  • AB 186 was unveiled Friday evening, August 28, 2026. It must pass both houses by midnight Monday, August 31. It is expected to pass.
  • Authored by Sen. Ben Allen and Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur, who also wrote the 2025 bill raising the program from $330 million to $750 million.
  • SB 122, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom on June 29, 2026, caps credits for any business at $5 million or 70% of total liability per year, whichever is greater, for three years. It was written to raise corporate tax revenue, not to target film.
  • Independent film, 10% of the $750 million program, is fully exempt from the cap. Major studio productions are not.
  • Refund election: current law gives cash instead of a credit against liability at a 10% discount over five years. AB 186 makes it a 5% discount over two years.
  • Carry-forward on credits earned under earlier program versions extends from 10 years to 15, per TheWrap. Variety describes the provision as extending the expiration of non-refundable pre-2025 credits by up to five years, protecting credits at risk of expiring after nine.
  • A provision easing claims against sales tax, sought by studios, was dropped from an earlier circulating version.
  • The MPA, the Entertainment Union Coalition and the Producers Guild of America signed on. Studio government affairs officials took part in negotiations, per TheWrap.
  • Kathleen Thompson, vice president of tax incentives at Cast & Crew: "It meaningfully improves the situation. They threw a bone to both the studios and to independents."
  • Zbur: the fix provides "greater stability and certainty" for production workers, and "does not address every challenge facing this highly competitive and mobile industry."
  • Deadline's account of the same bill calls it "AB136." Variety and TheWrap both give AB 186.

More than 750,000 audiobook titles were active in 2025, up 43% year over year, while U.S. audiobook revenue grew 9% to $2.43 billion, per the Audio Publishers Association. Audio rights that publishers once bundled into print deals without a separate price now draw competing bids from publishers, audio-first companies, podcast studios and platforms including Spotify and Amazon's Audible. Pushkin's Eric Sandler says there are now "real comps, and competition amongst bidders" on a right that five years ago went across with print at no stated value. Both statements can be true, and together they describe a right whose market price is rising faster than its negotiated price. That gap is the whole opportunity, and it stays open only until the bundling default breaks.
Specific Implication
Where a client's underlying literary property is being optioned, the audio right should be priced in that negotiation rather than assumed to have traveled with the print deal.
The Facts
  • More than 750,000 audiobook titles were active in 2025, up 43% from 2024, per the Audio Publishers Association. U.S. audiobook revenue grew 9% to $2.43 billion, slowing from 13% growth in 2024.
  • 58% of American adults, an estimated 157 million people, have listened to an audiobook, up from 51% or roughly 134 million a year earlier.
  • Eric Sandler, chief strategy officer at Pushkin Industries: "In publishing, audio has gone from being the piece nobody negotiated, and many still don't, to what can amount to an incredibly impactful part of the deal."
  • Sandler on the bidder set: publishers, audio-first companies, podcast studios and distribution platforms, with Spotify moving deeper into audiobooks alongside Audible.
  • Sandler on where leverage sits: "Leverage, meanwhile, follows the audience. Authors who bring listeners with them continue to have a leg up."
  • Kimberly Brower, founding partner and CEO of Park, Fine & Brower Literary Management, said audio has gone from something publishers wanted to control to something they "need to have."
  • Asked whether audiobooks have produced larger advances or higher valuations, Brower said sometimes, "but I have not seen it move the needle as much as one would think given how high audiobook sales have gotten."

Versant intends to repeat that across finance, news and entertainment. That makes Fandango's expansion structural rather than opportunistic.

Holders of finished films with an identifiable audience and available rights now have a distributor to approach that is not a studio and does not bid against them.

If Bonta Forces Paramount to Sell Cable Networks, the Analyst View Is That Almost No One Wants Them
Disney's A+E stake went at 4 times EBITDA. Paramount has been trying to sell BET for about five years. Comcast shuttered low-rated networks rather than sell them.
CEO Summary
California Attorney General Rob Bonta is pushing Paramount to divest cable networks as a condition of settling the antitrust case stalling its Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition. Scott Robson, senior research analyst at S&P Global Market Intelligence's Kagan group, told TheWrap the likely buyers are private equity and broadcast station groups, and that even those are hard to find: "It's hard to find a buyer for a depreciating asset." Bloomberg Intelligence estimates CNN, TBS and TNT could fetch roughly $8 billion together.
Why This Matters
The remedy may not be performable. Comcast's choice to shutter networks rather than sell them is a company revealing it valued those assets below the cost of a transaction, and Paramount's five-year failure to move BET says the same thing from the seller's side. Robson also raises the question a divestiture order would have to answer and usually does not: whether a sale conveys the linear feed alone or the content library behind it. Those are different assets, with different buyers and different prices.
Specific Implication
Anyone valuing a linear network should work from the 4x EBITDA A+E mark and confirm whether the backlog travels with the channel before pricing it.
The Facts
  • Talks between Paramount and the state attorneys general are in limbo. Bonta is pushing for divestiture of some combined-company networks.
  • Sector figures cited by Robson: cable network ad revenue down 10% year to date against 2025; carriage fee revenue down 3%; pay-TV subscriptions down from a 2012 peak above 100 million to roughly 60 million this year including virtual MVPDs such as YouTube TV. Citing a survey of homes keeping cable for sports, he said subscribers could fall another 30%.
  • Valuation marks: Disney's A+E Global Networks stake sold at 4 times EBITDA. Hearst bought Disney's 50% of A+E Global Media for $1.2 billion earlier this month. Bloomberg Intelligence puts CNN, TBS and TNT at roughly $8 billion combined.
  • Named potential buyers: private equity, plus broadcast station owners Hearst, Nexstar Media Group (The CW, NewsNation), E.W. Scripps (Ion) and Byron Allen's Allen Media Group (The Weather Channel).
  • On CNN: Barry Diller has expressed interest should it be for sale, and former CNN CEO Jeff Zucker, now at RedBird Capital, might bid. But Paramount CEO David Ellison wrote a New York Times op-ed this month asserting CNN ownership is at the heart of the merger challenges, and denied interest in selling it.
  • Robson on why Paramount holds: despite falling ratings, CNN and TNT generate the cash flow needed to pay down debt from the WBD purchase.
  • Robson: "Are they going to sell just the rights to the linear feed, or are they going to sell the entire backlog of content? Because those are two very different business models."
  • The expected roll-up never happened. After Comcast's 2024 and WBD's 2025 spinoff announcements, Netflix bid for WBD's streaming and studio assets but not its cable properties, and Versant said it wants linear below 50% of revenue.
  • Robson on Comcast shuttering networks: "It's like deeming them worthless."
  • In the same column's Deal Sheet: Arctos, a KKR-owned private equity firm, bought 10% of the Atlanta Falcons at a $10.6 billion valuation, its fourth NFL stake. Marc Shad agreed to buy control of the Minnesota Timberwolves and Lynx at a $4.5 billion valuation. DAZN is acquiring EverPass Media, holder of NFL Sunday Ticket commercial rights, terms undisclosed.

'Coyote vs. Acme' Opens Friday, Three Years After Warner Took a $30 Million Write-Off on It
Netflix, Amazon and Paramount all bid for the shelved film. Producer Chris DeFaria says Warner Bros. turned the offers down and would not let the bidders counter.
CEO Summary
"Coyote vs. Acme" opens in theaters Friday through Ketchup Entertainment, three years after Warner Bros. Discovery declared the completed film would not be released and took a $30 million tax write-off on it. The studio had done the same with a nearly finished "Batgirl" and the almost-complete "Scoob! Holiday Haunt." Producer Chris DeFaria and star Will Forte spoke to TheWrap about the period between.
Why This Matters
DeFaria draws the line where it belongs: studios abandon projects often, "but it's very unusual that that kind of process would govern a film that's finished. I've never seen that before in my life. That's the real change." Delivery used to be the point at which a filmmaker's exposure ended.

The resale detail is the sharper one. Offers came in from Netflix, Amazon and Paramount, the last with a theatrical component, and Warner declined them without permitting counters. A write-off is worth more to the owner than a sale only if no sale is allowed to establish a price.
Specific Implication
Release-obligation and reversion language should be tested against the case where a picture is complete and the owner declines to release or to sell, since that is now a documented outcome rather than a hypothetical.
The Facts
  • "Coyote vs. Acme" opens in theaters Friday, August 28, distributed by Ketchup Entertainment.
  • In November 2023 Warner Bros. Discovery said the film was fully completed but would not be released, shelving it for a $30 million tax write-off.
  • The studio previously shelved a nearly finished "Batgirl" and canceled the almost-complete animated "Scoob! Holiday Haunt."
  • DeFaria: "It was ordered by one regime at the studio and inherited by another. That's always rocky."
  • DeFaria: "It's very unusual that that kind of process would govern a film that's finished. I've never seen that before in my life. That's the real change."
  • After public outcry Warner pledged to shop the film. TheWrap reported in early 2024 that Warner executives called DeFaria wanting it off the books. Offers arrived from several studios and streamers including Netflix and Amazon, and Paramount proposed an ambitious theatrical component. Warner declined the offers and would not allow counters.
  • Forte: "It was confusion first. It cycled through a lot of stuff, a lot of confusion, which turned into just rage for a long time, and then just sorrow."
  • Forte, after a "funeral screening" on the Warner lot: "All of us after watching that movie were looking around at each other and saying, 'Is this the version that they saw that made them want to get rid of it?'"
  • The executives who made the decision, including CEO David Zaslav, had not watched the film.
  • Adapted from Ian Frazier's 1990 New Yorker story. James Gunn revived it at Warner in 2015 and holds producer and "story by" credit. Dave Green directed. Shot in New Mexico in 2022 with 180 local crew, 49 local principal actors and roughly 2,120 background talent. Cast includes Forte, Lana Condor, John Cena, Luis Guzmán and Eric Bauza. VFX and animation by DNEG.

Which Cable Networks Ellison Would Have to Sell to Settle With Bonta
Bonta told the Ankler Agenda the remedy targets the cable portfolio rather than CNN. WBD's cable arm earned $1.45 billion in second-quarter adjusted operating profit; Paramount's earned $1.06 billion.
CEO Summary
California Attorney General Rob Bonta told the Ankler Agenda podcast on Monday that a structural remedy, meaning a forced sale rather than a promise about conduct, would stop Paramount holding all 50 of the most sought-after US cable channels under one roof. Twelve state attorneys general are suing to block the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition. The Ankler surveyed more than half a dozen veteran cable executives on which networks David Ellison would fight to keep, which he could afford to lose, and who would buy the rest.
Why This Matters
The A+E sale to Hearst cleared north of $1 billion because Hearst owns roughly forty years of its own programming. Most Paramount and WBD channels do not own theirs. Comedy Central's remaining value sits almost entirely in The Daily Show and a 50 percent stake in South Park, both of which Ellison could move to Paramount+ and strip out.

That inverts the usual order of valuation. Nielsen rank says what a channel delivers this quarter. Rights ownership says what it is worth once the carriage deals end. Private equity, the buyer class sources name first, prices the second one.
Specific Implication
A producer with a series on a WBD or Paramount cable network should establish whether the network or the parent holds the underlying rights. That determines which entity a divestiture would put across the table.
The Facts
  • Bonta: "When it comes to cable channel licensing, a structural remedy means you can't have all 50 of the most sought-after channels in the United States of America; some other entity has to have control of those. That's what it means to have a structural remedy; you can't have them under the Paramount-Warner Bros. roof."
  • WBD holds seven networks in Nielsen's top 25: TNT, HGTV, TBS, CNN, TLC, Food Network and Discovery. Paramount earns more total linear revenue, largely on CBS, the most-watched network of 2025.
  • 66.1 million US households still subscribe to cable, per Evoca.tv, down 35 percent since 2010 and down from 68.7 million a year ago. Streaming is now nearly half of television viewing.
  • Paramount would carry an estimated $80 billion in debt at close. One source: "If I sell off my predominant revenue stream, what am I left with? A studio that might make or lose a little money? Is that a business?"
  • HBO Max has 140 million subscribers; Paramount+ has 79.6 million.
  • None of the executives surveyed believed Ellison would sell CNN.
  • Sources named TruTV and VH1 as the first to go. TNT and TBS are seen as too broad next to CBS, with sports the counterargument: they share NCAA tournament rights with CBS through 2032, so a merged company would hold the whole tournament. One source: "The only reason TNT and TBS exist is for live sports."
  • Disney's sale of its 50 percent A+E Global Media stake to Hearst brought north of $1 billion. Hearst owns the bulk of that programming outright.
  • Named exceptions with owned IP: TNT produced The Last Ship and Falling Skies, both recently charting on Netflix after WBD licensed them. Comedy Central produces The Daily Show and owns 50 percent of South Park with Trey Parker and Matt Stone.
  • Prior asking prices: Paramount turned down $3 billion for Showtime in 2023; Shari Redstone weighed a $1.6 billion BET sale in 2024; Paramount sought a stake buyer for MTV in January.
  • Named potential buyers: private equity ("holds on to declining assets with high and predictable revenue and milks them until the end"), Versant, Nexstar, Hearst, and Byron Allen's Allen Media Group, which bought a majority of BuzzFeed for $120 million in May.
  • Paramount statement: "Paramount remains hopeful and is committed to good faith discussions with Attorney General Bonta's office for an efficient resolution of our pending litigation."

CEO Summary

U.K. Producers Say Streamer Deals Cost Them the IP Rights Public Broadcasters Must Grant

CEO Summary
Belloni convened three senior U.K. producers at the Edinburgh TV Festival on Wednesday: Banijay U.K. CEO Patrick Holland, Nutopia CEO Jane Root, and Raw chief creative officer Dimitri Doganis. Under the U.K.'s Terms of Trade, set by the 2003 Broadcasting Act, the BBC and Channel 4 must grant independent producers the IP rights to their programs. The U.K. arms of Netflix and Amazon carry no such requirement. Doganis said producers who take those commissions work for hire and start from zero each year unless they have a returning series.
Why This Matters
Holland said the Banijay and All3Media merger gives him scale he has not yet used against the streamers: "The gun hasn't come out of the holster yet." That is supply-side consolidation held as unspent leverage on rights terms rather than spent on price. Doganis named the same lever more plainly, saying the only real leverage producers have is holding something a buyer wants. Neither said it has worked yet. The $1.2 million to $1.5 million ceiling Doganis put on Netflix true crime commissions suggests the buyer side is not pricing that leverage in.
Specific Implication
Representatives structuring star-led unscripted projects should test whether a YouTube-first launch preserves ownership that a streamer commission would extinguish.
The Facts
  • The panel: Patrick Holland (executive chair and CEO, Banijay U.K.; MasterChef, Big Brother), Jane Root (founder and CEO, Nutopia; Limitless With Chris Hemsworth, WWII With Tom Hanks), Dimitri Doganis (founder and chief creative officer, Raw; The Tinder Swindler, Trainwreck).
  • Belloni framed the stakes: the choice "could be worth billions of dollars to big production companies, which increasingly rely on the global exploitation of I.P. they own."
  • Holland said MasterChef, which started on the BBC, is now made in 70 territories and grew into "this huge I.P.-monetization machine" because the Broadcasting Act gave producers "skin in the game."
  • Editorial note in the piece: Netflix has said it buys U.K. programming almost exclusively from outside producers and offers deals on the U.K. model, but producers overwhelmingly choose buyouts upfront.
  • Doganis said Raw does not own a piece of the top-performing documentaries it makes for Netflix, calling that "an endless source of both pride and pain."
  • On Netflix's price for a true crime documentary, Doganis: "I would say they don't want to spend more than $1.2 million to $1.5 million, and they sometimes will, but they prefer less."
  • Doganis said the sports-documentary market "is definitely not as strong," with streamers moving into live sports instead because sports docs have diminishing returns.
  • Asked whether the All3Media merger lets Banijay demand a model change from Amazon, Netflix and Apple, Holland said: "The gun hasn't come out of the holster yet."
  • Doganis on producer leverage: make the business case that streamers are "sleeping on money" in dormant library titles, or "I've got something you really want, and you're not getting it unless..." He called the second "the only real leverage we have."
  • Root said Nutopia is making shows directly for YouTube and TikTok with Will Smith, Trevor Noah and Jeff Goldblum, brand-funded and owned jointly with the stars, with secondary sales to follow: "We'd own it with Trevor."
  • Doganis cited independently financed projects sold after completion (100 Foot Wave) and equity partners such as Fifth Season and Wiip as a route outside the work-for-hire model.
  • TV fees to the BBC and other public service broadcasters are declining, and the BBC's royal charter is up in 2027.
  • Disclosure carried in the piece: RedBird Capital, an investor in Banijay, is also an investor in Puck.

  • From the motion: "Twelve states have effectively vetoed a transaction that the other thirty-eight, and the United States, declined to challenge."

  • Norm Eisen, an attorney helping lead the #BlocktheMerger campaign: "There's no valid legal basis to do this." He said the states could file an amicus brief in Oakland instead.
  • The Supreme Court's original jurisdiction covers disputes between states such as boundaries and water rights. Iowa and Montana are not parties to the Oakland case.
  • The California AG's office said it was reviewing the filing.
  • Underlying case: the 12 states sued in July over competition in theatrical films, blockbuster films and basic cable. Trial is set for March 2, 2027; Paramount agreed to pause the merger until after it.

  • Bonta has said a settlement must include "robust structural remedies" in all three markets, such as asset sales. Paramount has not named any.

YouTube Offers 15 Creators Up to $10 Million to Stay Exclusive, and Hulu Joins the Bidding
YouTube is offering about 15 creators packages from the low seven figures to roughly $10 million for exclusivity, and telling them that leaving could cost them Brandcast stage time and preferred-ad-program status.
CEO Summary
YouTube is paying select creators to post exclusively to its platform, with offers out to around 15 names, according to multiple sources cited by Natalie Jarvey. Terms start in the low seven figures and reach roughly $10 million, in exchange for keeping videos off competing platforms for a defined period. Neal Mohan has not used this tactic before in his three years as CEO. It follows Netflix deals in July with Rhett & Link, the Stokes Twins and Nick DiGiovanni.
Why This Matters
There is now a stated price for creator exclusivity, and it was set by the buyer with the least reason to pay one. YouTube holds 13.8 percent of U.S. TV viewing against Netflix's 7.9 percent and still put eight figures on the table, which measures how far creator optionality has moved rather than how generous the platform is.

The threats are the more useful detail. Sources describe Brandcast stage time, billboard promotion and removal from the preferred advertising program as the consequences of leaving. Every one of those is discretionary promotion that no creator holds by contract today. A platform that had contractual hooks would use those instead.
Specific Implication
Creator representatives negotiating a YouTube exclusivity package should convert the promotional levers named here into committed terms, since Brandcast placement, billboard promotion and preferred-ad-program status are currently withheld at the platform's discretion.
The Facts
  • Offers are out to roughly 15 creators. Some are structured as guaranteed ad dollars, per one source.
  • Named as fielding offers: Kareem Rahma and Brittany Broski, plus Jesser, Cleo Abram and Michelle Khare (the latter three first reported by Bloomberg).
  • Sources describe retaliation for declining: no Brandcast stage, no billboard promotion, removal from the preferred advertising program YouTube runs for its top creators.
  • A YouTube spokesperson declined to comment.
  • A top dealmaker source: YouTube executives are "scared shitless"; "Inside YouTube, it's a mess; they're grasping at straws."
  • Netflix announced deals over a few days in July with Rhett & Link, the Stokes Twins, Alan Chikin Chow and Nick DiGiovanni, and added game show host Kevin Langue Wednesday. The deals include publishing videos on Netflix at the same time they go live on YouTube.
  • Hulu has offered at least one creator a seven-figure multi-year licensing deal and is planning a bigger creator push.
  • Disney ordered 20 episodes of family programming from Dhar Mann Studios on Friday. Amazon's Creator Services division has deals with Oprah and the Kelce brothers.
  • Nielsen, June: YouTube 13.8 percent of U.S. TV viewing, Netflix 7.9 percent.
  • Ted Sarandos called YouTube a "farm league" last year.
  • YouTube recently raised its monetization threshold and will start counting views at the moment playback begins rather than at 30 seconds.
  • Multiple creators were concerned by a fall 2025 algorithm change that reduced viewership and earnings. About 20 million videos are uploaded daily.
  • One exec in the space: "Fix your product and you don't have this problem."

Meta bought its way out of a trial that began eight days ago, and the price included a term binding companies that were not in the room. The states also secured an auditor with the right to raise concerns directly with them. Compliance stops being self-attested.

Anyone selling advertising or sponsorship against under-18 audiences on Instagram or Facebook should model inventory against limits Bonta says take effect within months, not against a multi-year appeals timeline.

YouTube Tells British Broadcasters It Is Not the Villain, and Attacks a UK Prominence Law
Pedro Pina became the first American tech executive to deliver the MacTaggart lecture, and used it to argue that a UK law guaranteeing public service media prominence on YouTube "would impair the public interest."
CEO Summary
YouTube EMEA vice president Pedro Pina delivered the James MacTaggart Memorial Lecture at the Edinburgh TV Festival on Wednesday, telling British broadcasters the platform is "not the villain" and that its move onto television screens is complementary to the BBC and Channel 4. He devoted the closing section of the 17-page speech to opposing UK government plans to compel YouTube and TikTok to promote public service content, which he called "forced prominence." He is the first person from an American tech giant to give the address.
Why This Matters
Pina argued the prominence rules would threaten "many UK-based creators and production companies," which puts independent producers rather than Google between the platform and the regulator. That is a reusable structure and it will show up in the next market that proposes the same rule. It also arrived on the day YouTube was reported to be paying creators up to $10 million for exclusivity and warning them about lost promotion if they leave.
The Facts
  • Pina: "A story is unfolding before our eyes. It is not a tragedy. And, as I hope I have shown you tonight, YouTube is not the villain." He invoked Aristotle: the tragic hero falls through hubris, not a villain.
  • Oxford Economics: 87 percent of Brits watch YouTube on their TV devices. Pina called this "complementary" to broadcasters.
  • Deadline's own analysis found YouTube overtook the BBC on a key measure of audience reach last year.
  • Pina praised The Traitors, Gavin & Stacey and The Great British Bake Off, and argued the industry is entering a "third golden age of television."
  • On the talent flow: "about a decade ago, TV producers spotted an opportunity. They saw that YouTube was effectively a database of up-and-coming talent, and lo and behold, TV started to poach big creators and shows."
  • On the UK proposal: "Forced prominence would impair the public interest, by unfairly shifting focus from independent creators and production companies, and by recommending that all our viewers watch the same things, disregarding personal taste."
  • He added it would risk "jeopardising the new talent pipeline, by undermining the creator economy, which contributes so much to UK soft power."
  • Pina said he shares "the concerns expressed about democracy and the public interest. But YouTube is a democracy by definition. A democracy of cultural production."
  • The BBC hired former Google executive Matt Brittin as director general and uses YouTube to reach younger audiences and stream news outside the UK.
  • Pina has worked at YouTube five years and is a British citizen. Previous MacTaggart speakers include James and Liz Murdoch, Mark Thompson and Louis Theroux.

Blake Lively Recovers $407,000 of the $8 Million in Fees She Sought From Baldoni
Judge Lewis J. Liman awarded $363,000 in fees and $44,000 in costs, and ruled that time spent on media relations and press coverage is not compensable.
CEO Summary
U.S. District Judge Lewis J. Liman ruled Wednesday that Blake Lively will receive about $407,000 in legal fees and costs following the settlement of her dispute with Justin Baldoni and Wayfarer Studios. She had sought just over $8 million. She claimed under a California statute protecting sexual harassment and discrimination claimants from retaliatory lawsuits. Liman found her counsel's rates reasonable in a case with "complex legal issues" but held the number of hours claimed was not, and limited recovery to defending the defamation claim.
Why This Matters
The court accepted the rates and cut the scope, which is where the money went. Liman held that Lively was "entitled only to the reasonable fees and costs necessary to defend against the defamation claim," and struck media-relations time entirely as "not integral" to that defense. Fee-shifting under this statute pays for the narrow act of defending the countersuit, not for the campaign that runs alongside it.
Specific Implication
Talent budgeting a retaliation defense should treat crisis communications as unrecoverable and raise who funds it at the outset, rather than assume a fee award will reach it.
The Facts
  • Award: $363,000 in attorneys' fees plus $44,000 in court costs, roughly $407,000.
  • Sought: $7.5 million in attorneys' fees plus about $540,000 in costs, just over $8 million.
  • Liman agreed with Baldoni and Wayfarer Studios that Lively was "entitled only to the reasonable fees and costs necessary to defend against the defamation claim."
  • On rates versus hours: counsel's rates "were not unreasonable" in a case with "complex legal issues," but "the number of hours for which Lively seeks reimbursement is unreasonable."
  • On media relations: "Media relations were not integral to defending the defamation claim brought against Lively. Accordingly, time spent on media relations and press coverage is not compensable."
  • Statutory basis: a California law protecting survivors of sexual harassment and discrimination from retaliatory lawsuits.
  • Lively filed in December 2024, alleging Baldoni and Wayfarer ran an online smear campaign after she raised harassment on the set of It Ends With Us. Baldoni and Wayfarer countersued for defamation and Baldoni also sued The New York Times. Both suits were dismissed, as were several of Lively's claims.
  • The parties settled the 18-month dispute in May, ahead of a federal trial scheduled for later that month. This was the last route to monetary compensation absent a new filing.

The parties describe an enterprise value of $111 billion, leaving the combined company more than $80 billion in debt, roughly $3 billion in annual free cash flow, and a synergy target above $6 billion. Synergy means combining functions; a settlement requiring separate operations forgoes it.
Why This Matters
Singer checks the most concrete commitment against Rentrak's release calendars. Warner Bros. has 19 films scheduled for 2027 and Paramount has 16. The pledge is being scored against zero rather than against what the two studios already planned to release.

Singer names the mechanisms that would make guarantees hold: escrowed funds, funded rather than pledged guarantees, more equity and less debt. Any party seeking output or employment protections should ask which of those is on the table.
The Facts
  • Deal economics as described by the parties: enterprise value $111 billion; more than $80 billion of debt on the combined company; roughly $3 billion in annual free cash flow; investment-grade commitment within a few years; synergy target above $6 billion.
  • The concrete commitment on the table: at least 30 theatrical releases a year, offered in writing to AMC, Regal and now other chains, potentially backed by penalties. The offered term runs three years.
  • Per Rentrak's release calendars: Warner Bros. has 19 films scheduled for 2027, Paramount has 16. For 2028 the two already have 22 films dated with slates still filling in.
  • Who wants a settlement: twelve state attorneys general, the Directors Guild and IATSE jointly, Cinema United, the three largest exhibitors, Gov. Gavin Newsom, likely successor Xavier Becerra and L.A. Mayor Karen Bass.
  • The Writers Guild's objection differs in kind: combining two major employers of writers reduces competition for writing services.
  • On synergies, Singer distinguishes benign savings (one software license, one headquarters lease) from those that eliminate a job, project, contract or line of spending, and asks which kind adds up to more than $6 billion at two companies that have already spent years cutting.
  • Los Angeles County's analysis identified thousands of exposed positions. Singer says his own analysis puts exposure considerably higher. Paramount argues a combined company would protect jobs better than two weaker ones.
  • Enforcement mechanisms Singer names: escrowed funds, funded rather than pledged guarantees, more equity and less debt. He observes each is available, each changes the deal's economics, and none has been offered.
  • One alternative he raises: Paramount owning both companies without integrating them.
  • Competitive spend benchmark cited: Netflix spends $20 billion a year on content.

Australia barred wholly AI-generated tracks from its charts and will make labels declare AI use
The rule takes effect Friday and follows an AI cover of Madonna's "Like a Prayer" that reached No. 4 on an ARIA singles chart.
CEO Summary
The Australian Recording Industry Association updated its charts code of practice to bar wholly AI-generated songs from its weekly charts and from ARIA Music Awards eligibility. Music made with generative AI qualifies only if it is "substantially human made" and "raises no stream or chart manipulation concerns." Tracks that used AI as a tool remain eligible. ARIA will require labels to mark each release as AI-generated or AI-assisted, using the taxonomy proposed last month by the IFPI and the RIAA.
Why This Matters
Enforcement sits with the distributor. ARIA has acknowledged it can identify generative-AI use only when a label tells it, so the rule works as a warranty the supplier signs rather than a test the chart runs.

Liability moves with the file. A label that certifies a release incorrectly loses chart and awards eligibility at once.
Specific Implication
Anyone drafting an AI clause should note who certifies here: the obligation, and the penalty, land on the delivering party rather than on the platform.
The Facts
  • The change takes effect Friday, via an update to the ARIA Charts code of practice.
  • Wholly AI-generated songs are barred from ARIA's weekly charts and from ARIA Music Awards eligibility.
  • Generative-AI music charts only if "substantially human made" and if it "raises no stream or chart manipulation concerns."
  • Songs where AI was used as a tool stay eligible.
  • ARIA will mandate the AI-generated and AI-assisted labels proposed last month by industry bodies including the IFPI and the RIAA.
  • Trigger: an AI cover of Madonna's "Like a Prayer" charted for weeks, reaching No. 4 on the Top 20 Australian Singles chart.
  • ARIA CEO Annaelle Herd: "Artists already use AI tools in their work, the Charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists' recordings is a different matter."
  • Herd: "a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent."
  • Per The Verge, ARIA admits it can only detect AI usage if "you tell us."
  • The move follows IFPI guidance last month for charts it manages across Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia, requiring music to be mostly human-made, free of manipulation concerns, and made on an AI service that is "properly authorised and lawful."
  • In the U.S., AI-generated music has appeared on Billboard's Hot Gospel Songs and Hot R&B charts.
  • Universal Music Group, Warner Music Group and Sony Music demanded a comparable framework last month, seeking "a clear boundary between human-led creativity and works that are purely synthetic or generated by unauthorized AI models."

A long-time supplier is suing Paramount's UK Channel 5 over a drama the network pulled during production
Blackbox Multimedia says it delivered the series and is owed money. Channel 5 says it never delivered and that it withdrew after a welfare complaint.
CEO Summary
Blackbox Multimedia, which produced The Ex-Wife and Benidorm is Murder for Channel 5, has issued proceedings against the Paramount-owned UK broadcaster over a crime drama that collapsed late in production this year. Blackbox says it met its contractual obligations and is owed payment. Channel 5 says the show was never delivered and that it pulled out after a person connected to the project said the drama was affecting their safety and wellbeing.
Why This Matters
The two sides do not agree on what the programme was. Blackbox will argue it developed the project into fiction, with no character or storyline representing a specific person; Channel 5 maintains it was a factual drama. Producers taking a true-events project into fiction should get the classification written into the commissioning agreement, since it determines who owns the clearance obligation.

  • Blackbox alleges the network wrongfully terminated its production deal and that money is owed.
  • Deadline: "It is highly unusual for a British producer to take legal action against a major buyer, let alone a long-term partner."
  • The drama collapsed at an advanced stage of production earlier this year. It was originally based on true events relating to abuse and criminal offenses. Neither party is specifying details, to protect the identity of a person involved.
  • Channel 5 pulled the series after a complaint from an individual connected to the project during production, who said the drama was affecting their safety and wellbeing.
  • Channel 5 says it was not made aware of these concerns by Blackbox before production, and that its duty of care to the complainant left it little choice.
  • Blackbox denies failing to raise concerns. It says it joined after Channel 5 and Spirit Studios developed the project, established that the complainant did not wish to participate, and alleges Channel 5 knew of that reluctance.
  • Blackbox will argue no character, relationship or storyline was based on or intended to represent any specific individual or case. Channel 5 maintains it was a factual drama.
  • Also party to the claim: Ex-Mas Movie Limited, a special purpose vehicle for the untitled drama, co-owned by Blackbox and Spirit Studios.
  • Blackbox is represented by Sheridans, Channel 5 by Lee & Thompson.
  • Jeremy Roberts of Sheridans: "Our clients delivered a programme in full compliance with their contractual obligations. They are pursuing their full entitlement through the courts."
  • A Channel 5 spokesperson: "We do not comment on ongoing legal matters."
  • Blackbox was co-founded by former Lionsgate UK COO Guy Avshalom and has delivered two seasons of The Ex-Wife, Benidorm is Murder, and 2023's The Castaways.

Lux Angeles Studios hired Binh Dang as head of production, completing an executive team that includes co-CEOs Matt Macur and Rebecca O'Hara, chair Steve Fabos, COO Lenny Vitulli, CRO Thomas Walton and creative executive Damien Douglas. The company is moving up toward independent features budgeted at $10 million to $20 million. Talent considering these projects is looking at Southeast Asian shoots, which changes location terms, crew composition and travel provisions in the deal.

  • Target band: independent features in the $10 million to $20 million range.

Shapiro notes the redacted complaint does not mention AI once. Any structural remedy the states win would bind the combined company across a production-cost base and a discovery layer that generative tools are widely expected to reshape inside the remedy's own life.

An arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to reinstate Karen Attiah with backpay, ruling the firing broke the union contract

CEO Summary
An independent arbitrator ruled that The Washington Post must reinstate columnist Karen Attiah with backpay and benefits, finding that her firing violated a collective bargaining agreement, according to the union and her legal team. Attiah said in September that she was terminated over social media posts following the assassination of Charlie Kirk. A Post spokesperson said the paper respects the arbitration process and declined further comment. The guild defended her in arbitration with support from the Democracy Defenders Fund.
Why This Matters
The ruling turned on contract language. Attiah's agreement permitted dismissal only through progressive discipline or for gross misconduct, and the firing cleared neither bar. Talent working under a discretionary morals or conduct clause has no equivalent remedy when an employer decides a public statement has become a liability.
Specific Implication
Anyone with a public political profile should check whether their agreement conditions termination on a defined cause standard or on a discretionary conduct clause. The two produce different outcomes on identical facts.
The Facts
  • Attiah's statement: "This decision confirms what we've said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion journalist, and doing that job is not misconduct."
  • Per the guild, Attiah could be terminated only as the "result of progressive discipline" or if conduct rose to "gross misconduct."
  • Post Guild Chair Natalie Vineberg said journalists "can't work at an organization where they must live in fear of being arbitrarily fired for doing their jobs," which in Attiah's case "was writing her opinion."
  • At the time of the firing the Post declined to comment on personnel matters and pointed to its policies and standards, including its social media policy.
  • Attiah joined the Post in 2014 and served a period as global opinions editor. She was the publication's last full-time Black opinion columnist and a prominent voice on the killing of columnist Jamal Khashoggi.

'Obsession' Crossed $500 Million Worldwide on a Sub-$1 Million Budget, the First Original Film of the 2020s to Get There
Focus Features acquired Curry Barker's "Obsession" out of a festival for a reported $15 million, and it has now grossed $501.5 million worldwide.
CEO Summary
Focus Features' horror film "Obsession" has finished its domestic run at $263.4 million and reached $501.5 million worldwide. It passes Pixar's "Elemental" at $494.6 million to become the top grossing original film since the pandemic. Writer-director Curry Barker made it for under $1 million. It opened to $17.1 million domestically and did not fall below that weekend figure until its sixth weekend in release. South Korea has not opened yet.
Why This Matters
Focus paid about $15 million for finished rights, The Ankler reported, roughly fifteen times the production cost. Sellers heading into Toronto and the fall markets have that number now.

What the money did not buy is the hold. Weekend grosses that climbed above the opening for a month came from audience word of mouth, and that is the variable no buyer can read off a festival screening.
Specific Implication
Sellers with a finished genre title should expect buyers to answer the "Obsession" comp by tying more of the price to performance, through escalators and box office bonuses rather than a larger guarantee.
The Facts
  • Worldwide gross $501.5 million: $263.4 million domestic, $238.1 million international, including $29.7 million in China and $26.7 million in the United Kingdom.
  • Previous top grossing original film since the pandemic: Pixar's "Elemental," $494.6 million.
  • TheWrap: highest grossing festival acquisition of all time, and the highest grossing film ever made for under $1 million.
  • The Ankler: Focus acquired it for $15 million; $37 million of the worldwide gross comes from territories Universal does not hold; second biggest R-rated horror film ever, behind "IT."
  • Domestic opening $17.1 million. Weekend totals ran higher than the opening for the following month and stayed above $17 million through five weekends.

Anna Paquin, Christy Carlson Romano and Melissa Gilbert each published statements this week calling for changes to how the industry treats child performers. Hayden Panettiere died last Sunday at 36, Michelle Trachtenberg died in February 2025 at 39, and Daveigh Chase died in July at 35. All three writers began working as children. Productions casting minors should expect on-set welfare and privacy terms to be raised in negotiation ahead of the next contract cycle rather than treated as a settled legal minimum.

The complaint does not rest on Western tropes. A pitch delivered to a producer's management company creates a dated record of access, and access is the element these claims are built on. Submission logs and rejection correspondence are the evidence on both sides of that question.

Karen Bass Wants the Paramount-Warner Merger Settled. Her Election Opponent Wants It Decided in Court.

CEO Summary
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass called Thursday for Paramount Skydance and California Attorney General Rob Bonta to settle the 12-state antitrust suit against the $111 billion Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, reversing her earlier opposition. Her general-election opponent, Councilmember Nithya Raman, said the same day that the merger's legality should be decided in court. Cinema United, the DGA and IATSE have all recently called for a settlement; WGA West publicly criticized Bass for joining them.
Why This Matters
Cinema United, the DGA, IATSE and now Bass all represent people who earn money when productions run, and a year of corporate limbo costs them whether the case is won or lost. WGA West and Raman represent the other side of the table, where one fewer studio buyer permanently changes what a writer can ask for.

Bass named the price of her support: "meaningful and enforceable commitments" on headquarters location, jobs, shoots and California investment. That is a settlement built on behavioral undertakings, meaning promises about conduct rather than a forced sale of assets.
Specific Implication
Any organization whose members are paid per production is a candidate to shift toward settlement next. Organizations that sell into a buyer market are not, and their public position is a reasonable proxy for how contested the March trial date remains.
The Facts
  • Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass held a press conference on Thursday, August 20, calling on Paramount Skydance and California Attorney General Rob Bonta to reach a quick settlement in the antitrust lawsuit filed by 12 state regulators against the $111 billion merger.
