Disney Holds 14 Release Dates In Rentrak For 2028 And Three Are Marvel
Disney holds 14 Rentrak dates for 2028 before counting 20th Century or Searchlight, and no wide release is currently dated against Pixar's Ghost Market or Incredibles 3.
CEO Summary
Deadline reports Disney has 14 release dates in the Rentrak system for 2028, excluding 20th Century Studios and Searchlight, with the year not yet fully slated. Three are Marvel titles: an untitled X-Men on May 5, Ghost Rider announced for 2028 without a date, and Black Panther 3 on December 15. The rest of the dated slate is Pixar original Ghost Market (March 10), live-action Tangled (March 31), live-action Lilo & Stitch 2 (May 28) and Incredibles 3 (June 16).
Why This Matters
An unnamed Disney executive told Deadline, of Sony's Marvel Studios co-production Spider-Man: Brand New Day at $1.8 billion and counting: "It's not about IP. It's about making great movies." That is a studio attributing a rival distributor's biggest-ever result to filmmaking rather than to the franchise, and the 2028 slate spends against that reading. Ghost Rider is Ryan Gosling with Shawn Levy directing. X-Men is Jake Schreier directing Adam Driver, Sadie Sink, Christopher Abbott and Samara Weaving.

Buying that caliber of filmmaker and cast into owned franchises costs more than the interchangeable-hire model Marvel ran for most of the last decade, and it moves negotiating power toward the director and lead rather than the property.
Specific Implication
Studios weighing 2028 tentpole dates are choosing between counter-programming and moving. Lionsgate currently has Resurrection of the Christ: Part Two on May 28 against Lilo & Stitch 2, and Universal has an untitled tentpole on December 20, five days after Black Panther 3.

The DGA Won A "Pilot Directed By" Credit With No Money Attached And Writers Are Furious
The DGA won the credit in about 10 hours across four or five sessions with TV studio heads, no labor lawyers present, and writers say they did not know it was on the table.
CEO Summary
The Directors Guild of America's June 2026 contract with the AMPTP created a "pilot directed by" credit that runs in every episode of every season of a series. It carries no compensation and no standardized placement, because studio heads could not agree on a universal position and pushed for case-by-case flexibility. Showrunners and writers, including dual DGA-WGA members, are calling it a power grab against the "created by" credit established 50 years ago.
Why This Matters
Creative rights are negotiated on a separate track from economics, without labor relations lawyers in the room. Per a source close to the negotiations, this provision took about 10 hours across four or five sessions between top TV directors and studio heads. Multiple writers told The Ankler they did not know it was under discussion, which is the practical cost of a side track nobody is watching.

Arrowverse co-creator Marc Guggenheim, a member of both guilds, described the effect precisely and admitted its limits: the credit "smacks a little bit of that balance of power shifting more and more away from TV showrunners to TV directors. Even though I can't really point to a concrete example of exactly how that credit moves the needle, I just feel the needle moving." Guggenheim's sharper complaint is aimed at his own guild, which he says has "the most narrowly defined, useless creative rights you can think of."
Specific Implication
Because placement was left to case-by-case negotiation, creators and pilot directors now have a series-level term to negotiate: whether the credit sits in the main title sequence or the end credits.
The Facts
  • The credit acknowledges the director of a show's first episode in every episode of every season going forward, with episodic directors credited separately. It has no compensation attached and is purely an onscreen credit.
  • Pilot directors are already paid well above scale, with residuals and other deal points negotiated by their agents.
  • The 2026 bargaining cycle produced no strikes. The WGA, SAG-AFTRA and the DGA all closed with the AMPTP, and all three extended their contracts from three years to four. The DGA closed in June, also winning health-plan and residual gains.
  • The DGA's creative rights committee was formed in 1964 under Frank Capra. Former DGA president Paris Barclay says the guild discussed the pilot-director issue internally for about 20 years before bringing it to studio negotiations for the first time this cycle.
  • Barclay, who has directed 10 pilots including Pitch, Station 19 and Doctor Odyssey and is also a WGA member: "My mother doesn't know Robert Butler. Robert Butler directed the pilots of Hill Street Blues, of Moonlighting, of Batman, did the first television miniseries, did Sisters, the family drama."
  • On the power-grab charge, Barclay: "It's hard to be a power grabber without getting any power. It's really about putting the facts out there and allowing them to be more public. It's not saying co-creator or anything like that."
  • A dual DGA-WGA member using the pseudonym "Drew" called it an "inelegant credit" and a "weird, closing-the-tent power grab by the DGA." Drew stands to receive it on his next show: "I don't really want it."
  • Former DGA president Tommy Schlamme says the committee consulted episodic directors before taking the idea to the table and got their blessing: "I hope it rises all boats."
  • Former DGA president Lesli Linka Glatter on writers: "They're your partner in telling the story. There's no sense of trying to take something away."
  • A showrunner cited the DGA's electronics transmission provision: he cannot get remote access to footage from set without director approval, and has had a director bar his assistant from sending shots from video village. Showrunners have no equivalent bill of rights.
  • Of the four new ongoing series with directing nominations at this year's Emmys, three nominees are nominated for the pilot episode: Hiro Murai (Widow's Bay), Vince Gilligan (Pluribus) and Andrew DeYoung (The Chair Company).
  • Residual resentment dates to 2023: the DGA ratified its contract in June 2023, a month after 11,000 WGA members struck and weeks before SAG-AFTRA's 160,000 performers joined.

Fifty Canadian Screen Bodies Are Fighting Carney's Review Of The Streamer Levy
Canada's regulator tried to raise the streamer levy from 5 percent of revenue to 15 percent in May, and the Carney government responded by putting the whole obligation under review.
CEO Summary
The 2023 Online Streaming Act obliges foreign streaming services to pay 5 percent of Canadian revenues into original production. Canada's media regulator moved to raise that to 15 percent in May 2026, and Mark Carney's Liberal government responded by saying the obligations should be reviewed because costs would be passed to subscribers. A coalition of 50 Canadian screen bodies, unions and festivals has written to Carney and culture minister Marc Miller urging them to "preserve the principle" that foreign streamers make "meaningful, predictable and enforceable" contributions.
Why This Matters
The coalition's letter rejects a specific alternative: an annual C$600 million (roughly $430 million) investment into production. That rejection is about structure, not size. A percentage-of-revenue levy scales with a platform's local business and can be enforced company by company; a fixed annual pot does neither, and it severs what a streamer contributes from what it earns in the market.

Deadline reports a perception inside Canada that the policy reversal is connected to the trade relationship with the Trump administration, while Carney maintains the concern is consumer pricing. Netflix, Prime Video and their peers have argued in multiple jurisdictions that they already invest without regulatory compulsion.
Specific Implication
Producers financing Canadian projects against a mandated local-spend floor should model the fixed-fund scenario, in which the buyer's obligation no longer grows with the buyer's Canadian revenue.
The Facts
  • The Online Streaming Act, introduced in 2023, set the obligation at 5 percent of revenues into original production.
  • Canada's media regulator moved to raise it to 15 percent in May 2026.
  • The Carney government said the obligations should be reviewed, citing pass-through to subscribers.
  • A coalition of 50 major Canadian screen bodies, unions and festivals sent an open letter to Carney and culture minister Marc Miller.
  • The letter broadly rejects an alternative annual C$600M (roughly $430M) production investment.
  • Signatories: "Instead of building and sharing our own stories with the world, we would be left watching from the sidelines as foreign content increasingly defines what Canadians see on their screens."
  • Canada is the production home of Heated Rivalry, which Deadline describes as television's biggest recent hit.

Jeanie Buss Says The Lakers Stake Sale To Iger And Kushner Is A "False" Report
ESPN reported the six Buss siblings voted to sell their 17.8 percent Lakers stake to the Iger group; hours later Jeanie Buss's attorney called the report false and cited a 2017 court order naming her controlling owner for life.
CEO Summary
On August 12, Lakers owner Mark Walter disclosed an agreement to sell the franchise to a group led by Thrive Capital's Joshua Kushner and former Disney CEO Bob Iger at a reported $12.5 billion valuation, pending NBA board of governors approval. On Monday, ESPN's Shams Charania reported the Buss family trust had voted to sell its remaining 17.8 percent stake to that group, and the siblings issued a family statement confirming it. Jeanie Buss's attorney Adam Streisand disputes the report and demands her siblings take no action on the vote.
Why This Matters
The disputed stake does not decide the sale. Per The Hollywood Reporter, even if Jeanie Buss blocks the family's stake from moving, that would not affect the Walter transaction. What it decides is her role, and the governing document is not the purchase agreement but a 2017 court order fixing her as controlling owner for her lifetime absent a further order modifying the trust.

Iger's position is the part with reach beyond basketball. He is at Thrive Capital, and his named operating assignment after close is a sports franchise. That was disclosed five days before he was honored as a Disney Legend at D23.
Specific Implication
Legacy family stakes carried through a control transaction should be treated as a succession-instrument question, not a purchase-agreement question. The Buss dispute is running through a nine-year-old probate order and a press leak.
The Facts
  • Walter bought control of the Lakers in a deal that closed last October at a $10 billion valuation. The August 12 agreement to sell to the Kushner/Iger group carries a reported $12.5 billion valuation.
  • Kushner, 41, leads Thrive Capital and would be controlling owner in his personal capacity if the NBA board of governors approves. Iger works at Thrive and is expected to have a significant operational role after close.
  • Charania reported the trust of six siblings voted to relinquish its 17.8 percent stake. Deadline reports four of the six siblings voted for the sale, and that the stake would take Iger and Kushner from roughly 65 percent to 83 percent.
  • Buss family statement to ESPN, unsigned: "We have decided as a family to sell the remaining Buss Family Trust shares to the Bob Iger group as part of the ongoing transaction. We love the Lakers, Laker fans and will continue to support Los Angeles; but it is time to use this opportunity to move on and exit gracefully while we still can."
  • Adam Streisand, for Jeanie Buss: "Shams Charania of ESPN falsely reported that the six Buss siblings voted to sell the 17.8% ownership stake in the Lakers to Josh Kushner and Bob Iger, and that my client, Jeanie Buss, is 'out' as controlling owner. This is just the latest instance of a years-long pattern whereby Joey and Jesse Buss leak false, defamatory and pernicious 'information' to Mr. Charania."
  • Streisand's demand: "I demand that your clients make clear publicly that Jeanie Buss is the Controlling Owner of the Los Angeles Lakers and that your clients shall take no action on this supposed 'vote' to sell the 17.8% stake."
  • When Walter acquired the team, he agreed to keep Jeanie Buss as governor for five years, after which he holds an option to buy out the family stake.
  • Deadline notes NBA rules require a governor to own at least 15 percent of a team.
  • Iger, quoted by Deadline from The California Post: "We have enormous respect and appreciation for Jeanie, her father and what they've contributed to this franchise. And we have every intention to honor the agreement that was made between Mark and Jeanie."
  • Dr. Jerry Buss bought the Lakers, the L.A. Kings and the Forum in 1979 and died in 2013. The family holds 11 NBA championships across 46 years. CNBC first reported the Streisand letter.

The pressure behind the deliberate pace is dated. Peacock Is Testing A Loyalty Program That Pays Subscribers In Pizza And Groceries
Peacock's new tiers are Gold, Platinum and Diamond, set purely by how many years someone has subscribed, and the launch rewards are an Instacart+ membership, a Pizza Hut code and shop discounts.
CEO Summary
Peacock launched a beta membership program on August 17 for a randomly selected group of Premium and Premium Plus subscribers. Members are sorted into three tiers by subscription tenure: Gold at three months to one year, Platinum at one to three years, Diamond at three-plus years. Peacock has 48 million paid subscribers and posted its first quarterly profit in Q2 2026, six years after launch, as NBCUniversal prepares to separate from Comcast over the next 12 months.
Why This Matters
Every launch reward comes from outside the entertainment product. A grocery-delivery subscription, a pizza code and merchandise discounts cost Peacock partner economics rather than programming dollars, which is a way to defend a subscriber base without reopening a content budget at the exact quarter the service first cleared profitability.

The tier design is the substantive part. Status is keyed to years subscribed, not to spending or hours watched, which makes cancellation a forfeiture of accrued standing rather than a neutral monthly decision. Peacock's stated roadmap extends that logic into assets no other streamer holds, naming Universal Parks perks and early access to NBCUniversal live events.
Specific Implication
Early access to live events and content previews are availability rights. Rightsholders negotiating NBCUniversal live-event or premiere terms should expect a subscriber-tier carve-out to be requested.
The Facts
  • Open to a randomly selected group of Peacock Premium and Premium Plus subscribers.
  • Tiers by tenure: Gold (three months to one year), Platinum (one to three years), Diamond (three-plus years).
  • Launch benefits: 25 percent discount at NBCU Shop for all members; Bravo Shop discounts of 15 percent (Gold), 20 percent (Platinum) and 25 percent (Diamond); a complimentary one-year Instacart+ membership; and a Pizza Hut digital code for a free second medium pizza.
  • The Pizza Hut code is a limited-time offer unlocked after streaming three movies, the only content-linked mechanic at launch.
  • Instacart+ benefits named: no grocery delivery fees with a $10 minimum basket, a complimentary New York Times Cooking subscription, and family sharing with up to three people.

Sony Walked From "The Salt Path" In The Week It Was Signing US Distribution
Gillian Anderson says Sony pulled out of the US distribution deal the same week the Observer reported the memoir behind the film was misrepresented; the film placed a year later with Rialto Distribution International.
CEO Summary
Anderson, who starred opposite Jason Isaacs in The Salt Path, told The Times of London that Sony withdrew from a US distribution deal after the UK's Observer reported last summer that key elements of the Ray and Moth Winn memoir were misrepresented. Both the book and the film were billed as a true story. The film now has a North American release through Rialto Distribution International later this month.
Why This Matters
Anderson: "The story came out the week we were signing U.S. distribution and Sony withdrew." No litigation and no formal finding is described. Press reporting alone was enough for a major to exit at the signing table, on a completed film that Variety's pre-scandal review had praised.

Anderson also identified where the process failed, and it was not at the rights chain: "I was interested in the due diligence -- like, how has it come to this? What degree of proof was there? They had told us that they couldn't talk about [a previous] legal case because it was ongoing." The authors' deflection on a prior legal matter went unexamined while the factual claim the marketing rested on went untested.
Specific Implication
Acquirers and financiers on memoir or life-rights projects should diligence the accuracy of the underlying account as a separate item from chain of title, and should expect the walk-away trigger to be a news report rather than a court finding.
The Facts
  • The Salt Path is based on the memoir by Ray and Moth Winn, telling of a couple who walk the south coast of England after their home is repossessed and Moth is diagnosed with a terminal illness. Anderson played Ray; Isaacs played Moth. Both book and film were billed as a true story.
  • Last summer the Observer reported that key elements had been misrepresented: that the couple lost their house after Ray embezzled money, casting doubt on Moth's diagnosis of corticobasal degeneration (average survival eight years), and that the couple's names were pseudonymous. The Winns, who won numerous awards for the book, disputed the allegations at the time.
  • Anderson: "It was really disappointing, a huge letdown. ... We had been so surprised by its success: 'What, really, this film about two old people going on a walk?' It felt like such a betrayal because we'd spent time with [the Winns]."
  • Anderson has not heard from the couple and expressed some sympathy: "It must have been really unsettling, to be potentially, allegedly, not telling the truth on live TV."
  • Variety exclusively reported earlier this year that the film would get a North American release via Rialto Distribution International. Rialto CEO Kelly Rogers at the time: "This is a film of quiet power. It speaks to something deeply human -- love, endurance and the idea that it's never too late to begin again."
  • Variety's review, published before the scandal broke, said the film "makes it worth the emotional investment."
  • A representative for Sony did not respond to Variety by press time.

TikTok Shop Is Poaching WhatNot Sellers Over A Thirty-Cent Transaction Fee
TikTok representatives met repeatedly with WhatNot candy seller Taylor Lally, who says the negotiation is about WhatNot's flat thirty-cent-per-transaction fee, not audience.
CEO Summary
WhatNot raised hundreds of millions of dollars in July at a $20 billion valuation, on $8 billion of goods sold in 2025. TikTok Shop has emerged as its principal rival, offering sellers a 100 million-plus US user base. Both platforms are now recruiting individual auction hosts directly, and the seconds-long single-item auction format WhatNot popularized has already been copied across platforms.
Why This Matters
The format is not the moat. WhatNot's bidding mechanic is now standard on TikTok Shop and elsewhere, which leaves the sellers themselves as the contested asset, and explains why platform representatives are meeting individual hosts rather than competing on features. Lally's leverage against a flat fee is that a rival wants him.

Hosting is also becoming a priced skill. In a survey commissioned by Adobe, 30 percent of live shoppers said their purchase decisions were driven in part by the identity of the host. Lally is hiring a second host to extend his broadcast hours, and eBay built a service earlier this year for camera-shy sellers to hire livestream hosts.
Specific Implication
There is a paid on-camera market forming with no studio gatekeeper, a measurable conversion metric, and a negotiable take rate. The commercial term to watch in these moves is the per-transaction fee.
The Facts
  • WhatNot raised hundreds of millions in July 2026 at a $20 billion valuation and continues adding verticals including food and golf. It says it sold $8 billion of goods in 2025.
  • Total US e-commerce sales topped $1.3 trillion in the same period, per US Census Bureau data. Chinese buyers spend hundreds of billions of dollars annually on live shopping.
  • TikTok Shop lets sellers go live to the app's 100 million-plus user base.
  • Taylor Lally, who sells candy in ultra-fast single-item auctions, says he will cross $1 million in sales this year. He works "12- to 16-hour days" around a four-hour live window.
  • Lally on the negotiation: "A big deal about WhatNot, which we can't really get around, is a thirty-cent transaction fee, regardless of what we sell. So it's just negotiating those terms with TikTok." TikTok representatives reached out and met with him multiple times.
  • Lally nearly shut his account down last year until another seller advised switching to seconds-long single-item auctions: "This kind of totally changed how we do business."
  • Seller and advisor Kip Roland on the $1 opening bid: "If you start something that's $1 but it's actually worth $50, people aren't asking themselves, 'Should I buy it?' They're asking themselves, 'What am I willing to spend on it?'"
  • Roland reached 40,000 viewers selling World Cup jerseys in June with a little over 13,000 followers: "The algorithm recognized that people were staying for a long time, they were converting to buyers, they were engaging, and so it just pushed it to more and more and more people."
  • StockX co-founder Josh Luber: "Ultimately, all marketplaces live and die on liquidity, and TikTok is going to have the most liquidity from day one. It's a question of can they convert them over to be consumers."
  • Adobe-commissioned survey: 30 percent of live shoppers said their purchasing decisions were driven in part by the identity of the host.
  • Jimmy Donaldson (MrBeast) went live on WhatNot on Super Bowl Sunday under a partnership with the company, giving away items including a Birkin bag and a Lamborghini. Livestreaming consultant Ashley Christenson: "Anytime Jimmy's paying attention and testing something, it's worth looking at."

CEO Summary
Summer 2026 domestic box office stands at $4.24 billion, up 24 percent on 2025 and 6 percent above 2019, per Rentrak. Full-year 2026 is at $6.9 billion, up 19 percent year over year and 6 percent below 2019. The gain is concentrated in the summer: only "GOAT" crossed $100 million domestic in January and February, and it barely did so.
Why This Matters
Two months of the calendar are producing almost nothing while the rest of the year runs ahead of a record comparison. In the same January and February of 2019, four films cleared $100 million domestic and at least three more landed between $50 million and $100 million. Nothing in the 2026 figures suggests audiences behaved differently in those weeks; studios released different films into them.

That makes the remaining gap to 2019 a supply question rather than a demand question. The 6 percent shortfall for the full year sits almost entirely in a window where the competitive set is thin by the industry's own scheduling choices.
Specific Implication
For a mid-budget title choosing a date, the January and February corridor currently offers the weakest competitive field on the calendar, and the 2026 results show what happens when nothing wide is dated into it.

Producers are reading sample scripts without cover pages to judge them on the material rather than on prior working relationships.
Why This Matters
The blind read is the part that carries information beyond this one room. Producers strip cover pages when the name-based shortlist has stopped narrowing the field, which happens once the qualified pool is far larger than the number of seats. Goldberg reported last year that hundreds of submissions per staffing room had become normal after Peak TV; sources say this volume still surprised everyone involved.

One source attributes the DCC volume partly to the market and partly to the title: "people wanting to be on cool IP."
Specific Implication
Where a room is being read cover-page-blind, the submitted sample is doing the work a relationship normally does, which changes what a writer without existing producer relationships should prioritize in a submission.

Disney Turned Down Adam Driver's Star Wars Movie, Then Cast Him As The X-Men Villain
Ten months of fan pressure, a banner plane over the Burbank lot, two Times Square billboards and a skydiver did not reopen the project. Filoni: "It's not here, you won't find it here."
CEO Summary
Lucasfilm co-President Dave Filoni told Deadline at D23 that Adam Driver's Kylo Ren project, The Hunt for Ben Solo, is not in development. The film was developed by Driver with director Steven Soderbergh and rejected by then-CEO Bob Iger and Disney Entertainment co-Chairman Alan Bergman. On the same D23 stage, Disney confirmed Driver as Mister Sinister in Marvel Studios' X-Men, dated May 5, 2028.
Why This Matters
Disney resolved both questions about Driver in the same 24 hours, and the answers point the same direction. It will buy a marquee actor into a role the studio controls. It will not fund the project that actor originated, even with a director of Soderbergh's standing attached and a decade of audience affection behind the character.

The reasoning Disney gave is worth holding onto. Iger and Bergman objected that the character died in The Rise of Skywalker, though Darth Maul, Boba Fett and Emperor Palpatine were all revived after on-screen deaths in the same canon. A continuity rule applied selectively is a preference expressed as a rule.
Specific Implication
An actor or filmmaker developing an originated project inside a Disney franchise should establish early where the greenlight sits. Deadline's reporting places the Ben Solo decision with Iger and Bergman rather than with Lucasfilm, which ran the development.
The Facts
  • Filoni at D23, asked whether Kylo Ren returns: "It's not here, you won't find it here. The force is not with us in that regard; I love the love you feel for it."
  • The Hunt for Ben Solo was set after Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker and would have put the character on a redemptive path. Driver disclosed the rejection in an October 2025 AP interview.
  • Fan campaign: a banner plane over Disney's Burbank lot after the November earnings call, two Times Square billboards on January 3 and 5, a skydiving stunt in March, and digital trucks at the Mandalorian and Grogu premiere and San Diego Comic-Con.
  • X-Men casting confirmed at D23: Driver as Nathaniel Milbury / Mister Sinister, Christopher Abbott as Professor X, Inde Navarrette as Rogue, Maya Boyd as Storm, Samara Weaving as Emma Frost, Kit Connor as Cyclops. Directed by Jake Schreier, written by Lee Sung Jin and Joanna Calo. Release date May 5, 2028.
  • Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu, which Filoni co-wrote and produced, finished at $345 million worldwide.

Netflix's Answer To Tyra Banks: She Signed Away The Edit
Netflix's 28-page motion does not lead with accuracy. It leads with the contract: "Banks expressly agreed those decisions belonged to the filmmakers." Her lawyer is demanding the unedited interview be released.
CEO Summary
Netflix filed an anti-SLAPP and dismissal motion in Los Angeles Superior Court on August 14 against Tyra Banks's defamation suit over the docuseries Reality Check: Inside America's Next Top Model. Banks filed in June alleging a false narrative built through what she called surgical editing. Netflix is seeking an October 30 hearing and is represented by Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher.
Why This Matters
The motion is the clearest public statement yet of how a major platform intends to use a documentary participation release. Netflix is arguing that the release assigns editorial judgment to the filmmakers, and that a subject who signed it cannot later sue over sequencing, omission or emphasis. If the court accepts that framing, the release becomes a near-complete defense to this class of claim.

Tom Clare's response reveals where the pressure actually sits. He is not asking for creative control. He is asking Netflix to release the complete unedited interview, which is a demand about evidence rather than about editorial rights. That is a strong indication that a raw-footage or preservation clause is the term that decides these disputes, not the accuracy language.
Specific Implication
A subject negotiating participation in an archival documentary should treat access to their own raw interview as a term to secure at signing. Clare's statement shows that after release, the footage sits with the platform and the subject must litigate to see it.
The Facts
  • From the motion: "Documentary filmmakers decide whom to interview, what to ask, which answers to include, how to sequence competing accounts, and what to leave on the cutting-room floor. Banks expressly agreed those decisions belonged to the filmmakers. Dissatisfaction with editorial judgments is not actionable defamation."
  • Also from the motion: "Strip away the Complaint's rhetoric of 'manipulation' and 'surgical editing,' and Banks's theory reduces to a request for more airtime and an edit more to her liking."
  • Netflix spokesperson: "Tyra Banks was given the opportunity to speak openly about her experience and the creators fairly presented her perspective alongside those of every other participant shown in this documentary."
  • Banks's attorney Tom Clare: "Netflix has Tyra's complete, unedited interview. If Netflix stands behind the accuracy of its documentary, it should release that interview in full and let viewers judge for themselves."
  • Banks filed on June 13, 2026. Netflix filed on Friday, August 14, 2026.

Disney Dated Eleven Titles Through 2029 At D23 And One Of Them Is Original
Coco 2 lands November 2029, Tangled live-action March 31, 2028, Zootopia 3 March 2028, Lilo & Stitch 2 May 28, 2028. Pixar's Ghost Market is the only title on the list not built from something Disney already owns.
CEO Summary
Disney used its D23 showcase in Anaheim on August 14 and 15 to date a theatrical slate running to November 2029. The announced titles include Hexed (November 25, 2026), Ice Age: Boiling Point (February 5, 2027), Gatto (March 5, 2027), The Bluey Movie (August 6, 2027), Tangled live-action (March 31, 2028), Zootopia 3 (March 2028), X-Men (May 5, 2028), Lilo & Stitch 2 (May 28, 2028), Incredibles 3 (summer 2028), Ghost Market (2028) and Coco 2 (November 2029). Disney+ also greenlit a Kingdom Hearts series with game creator Tetsuya Nomura attached.
Why This Matters
A studio that dates a title three years out has already committed the money, the director and most of the cast. So the useful reading of this list is not what Disney is excited about. It is what Disney has already decided it is willing to be locked into, and the answer is continuation work on assets it owns or acquired.

The Kingdom Hearts order is the one structural departure. It brings a licensed Square Enix property to Disney+ and Disney Channel with the original game's creator attached, rather than adapting something from the Disney library. That is a different rights posture from the rest of the slate and a different set of partners.
Specific Implication
A filmmaker or writer targeting a Disney theatrical slot in this window is competing for assignment work on an established property. The one original theatrical berth on the announced list is Pixar's, and it is already filled.

Europe's Broadcasters Are Merging Into National Champions Because The 16-34s Are Gone
U.K. public-service viewing among 16-to-34-year-olds fell from 95 minutes a day in 2015 to 21 in 2025. Over the same decade the median cost per minute of U.K. high-end scripted rose about two-thirds.
CEO Summary
Sky has agreed to buy ITV's broadcast and streaming operations for $2.1 billion. RTL is combining its German free-to-air network with Sky Deutschland, and MediaForEurope has taken control of ProSiebenSat.1 alongside Mediaset and Telecinco. On the production side, Banijay and All3Media merged in an $8.5 billion deal. French regulators blocked the equivalent move when TF1 and M6 abandoned a $4.1 billion merger in 2022.
Why This Matters
Enders Analysis estimates a combined Sky and ITV would hold 18.3 percent of U.K. TV and streaming viewing against YouTube's 18.6 percent. That number defines the ceiling of this strategy. The largest possible merger in the largest European commercial market produces a company that is still second to a single platform it cannot acquire, regulate or outspend.

RTL's Clement Schwebig describes the German combination as bringing his company "within striking distance of Netflix and Amazon in this market." The qualifier is doing the work. These are national plays in national markets, competing against companies for which each of those markets is a segment.
Specific Implication
Anyone pricing European rights territory by territory should expect the number of independent bidders per market to fall in the U.K., Germany, Italy and Spain over the next two cycles. Only France has so far held the line through regulation.
The Facts
  • Sky (Comcast-owned) agreed to acquire ITV's broadcast and streaming operations in the U.K., valued at $2.1 billion.
  • RTL is combining its market-leading German free-to-air broadcaster with Sky Deutschland, the country's No. 1 pay-TV group, acquired from Comcast.
  • MediaForEurope, controlled by the Berlusconi family, took control of ProSiebenSat.1, Germany's No. 2 commercial network, adding it to Mediaset in Italy and Telecinco in Spain.
  • Banijay and All3Media completed an $8.5 billion production merger.
  • U.K. daily viewing of public service broadcasters fell from 153 minutes per person in 2015 to 88 minutes in 2025. Among 16-34s it fell from 95 minutes to 21.
  • French linear viewing among 25-49s has more than halved since 2015. German daily viewing among 14-69s has fallen sharply since 2019.
  • U.K. median budget per minute for high-end scripted TV rose roughly two-thirds over the past decade. French drama hourly cost, excluding soaps, rose 66 percent between 2015 and 2024.
  • Combined RTL+ and Sky Deutschland: about 12.4 million paid subscribers, third-largest streamer in German-speaking Europe. RTL/Sky advertising reaches nearly 69 million German homes, 87 percent of the population.
  • Enders Analysis on a combined Sky/ITV: about 31 percent of U.K. broadcast TV viewing, roughly 18 percent of total video viewing including streamers and YouTube, about 20 million U.K. households weekly against Netflix's 16 million.
  • Enders Analysis' Cleodie Kilgour: "Broadcasters must achieve true scale to remain competitive."
  • Sky CEO Dana Strong on the ITV deal: "Brands want digital, they want choice, they want more digital advertising capability powered by data."

Disney Spent A Century Suing Fan Creators. Now It Is Licensing Them On TikTok.
Disney's Eric Schrier put the "Verts" short-form push on Disney+ in the same sentence as Dan Fogelman: "Creators are just storytellers." ESPN reached 640 million digital and social users in June.
CEO Summary
At D23 on August 14, Disney executives described a pact signed with TikTok the previous week that encourages fans to make clips using authorized Disney IP. Variety noted the reversal for a company that has historically enforced its copyright and trademark rights vigorously. On the same panel, Direct-to-Consumer International president Eric Schrier called Disney+'s vertical microdrama push a significant investment.
Why This Matters
Disney's rights posture has been the industry's reference point for a century, and it has been enforcement. Authorizing third parties to build with Disney characters on a platform Disney does not own inverts that. The company is now treating fan production as distribution rather than as infringement.

The consequence runs past Disney. Every rights holder benchmarking a creator-licensing term now has a live comparable set by the most protective owner in the business. That is a floor that did not exist a month ago.
Specific Implication
An IP owner negotiating creator-licensing terms on a third-party platform can reference the Disney and TikTok arrangement as a precedent for what an authorized-use grant looks like at the most conservative end of the market.
The Facts
  • Eric Schrier is Disney's president of Direct-to-Consumer International Originals, Strategic Programming and Emerging Media. Erin Teague is executive VP of Product Management for Disney Entertainment and ESPN. The panel was moderated by former YouTube and Instagram executive Jon YouShaei and included creator Blake Silva.
  • Schrier: "We've always looked at making film and television in very finite formats. Half hours, hours, feature length films. And now you can tell any story. Creators are just storytellers."
  • Teague: "There will never be a replacement for that long-form original content but what is interesting is the way that it is now being supplemented by the shorter form analysis, the clips."
  • Teague: "Next generations of fans are expecting more from their entertainment experience. They want to be a part of the story... They want to have more agency in the storytelling experience with the democratization of creativity."
  • ESPN's head of global sports and talent office Freddy Rolón: ESPN runs 43 linear networks in more than 130 countries and territories, is on Disney+ in more than 100 markets, and reached 640 million digital and social users in June.
  • Rolón: "We reach more casual fans, we reach more female fans on Disney+ and then on the flip side, ESPN brings to Disney+ a credibility about sports."

Spider-Man: Brand New Day holds No. 1 for a third weekend with an estimated $67 million and crosses $2 billion worldwide on Sunday, the eighth film to do so. The Odyssey passed $500 million domestic in its fifth weekend. Warner Bros. and Bad Robot's The End of Oak Street is estimated at an $18.7 million opening against a reported $80 million budget, at the low end of Warner's own projections.
Why This Matters
The weekend is usually read as franchise versus original, but The Odyssey breaks that frame. It is an R-rated original heading past $1.5 billion worldwide and toward the all-time R-rated domestic record. The variable separating it from The End of Oak Street is not IP. It is whether the director's name functions as the title.

That distinction matters more than the aggregate numbers, because it is the one a studio can act on. A studio can buy a brand-name director. It cannot manufacture one, which is why the price for the roughly two dozen filmmakers who clear that bar keeps rising while everything else in the original lane gets harder to finance.
Specific Implication
A packager pitching an original theatrical feature in the next cycle should expect buyers to cite the $80 million against $18.7 million comparison. The counter is the director's own opening history, not the genre or the cast.

Disney Held Mandalorian And Grogu For 103 Days To Protect A $345 Million Run
The film opened to $167 million globally on Memorial Day and finished at $345 million on a $165 million negative. Disney+ gets it September 2, three and a half months later.
CEO Summary
Disney set September 2, 2026 as the global Disney+ date for Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu, a 103-day gap from theatrical release. The Jon Favreau film is the lowest-grossing live-action Star Wars title. It scored 60 percent with critics and 86 percent with audiences. Lucasfilm's next theatrical release is Star Wars: Starfighter, set for Memorial Day 2027 with Shawn Levy directing and Ryan Gosling starring.
Why This Matters
Studios shorten windows on titles that disappoint, because the theatrical upside is gone and the streaming benefit is immediate. Disney did the opposite here and held for 103 days. That is a choice to protect the window as policy rather than to optimize this particular title.

The read on the film itself is in Lucasfilm's next move. Starfighter is set in a new galaxy with no Skywalkers, a movie star in the lead and a director who came from a Marvel-scale hit. Lucasfilm's response to a series-derived feature underperforming is a feature that owes nothing to the series slate.
Specific Implication
Talent with a theatrical-gross-based backend on a streaming-derived feature should model the window as a term the studio will hold for policy reasons. A long window on an underperforming title compresses the participation base without accelerating any streaming-side compensation.
The Facts
  • Disney+ global streaming date: September 2, 2026. Gap from theatrical release: 103 days.
  • Opening: $167 million globally over Memorial Day weekend. Final worldwide: $345 million. Production cost before P&A: $165 million.
  • Reception: 60 percent with critics, 86 percent with audiences.
  • Luminate records the 2026 domestic cume at $177,730,064.
  • Directed by Jon Favreau. Co-written by Favreau, Noah Kloor and Lucasfilm co-President Dave Filoni. Produced by Ian Bryce, Kathleen Kennedy, Favreau and Filoni. Cast includes Pedro Pascal, Sigourney Weaver, David Allen White and Martin Scorsese.

  • Deadline's assessment: "Moviegoers essentially didn't want to go out of their way to see a streaming property on the big screen."

Disney And Epic Turned A Theme Park Queue Into A Fortnite Mission
The Smuggler's Run cockpit was built on Unreal Engine years ago, which is why ride assets can now appear inside Fortnite. Complete the queue mission in Orlando or Anaheim and the outfit unlocks in the game.
CEO Summary
Disney and Epic Games unveiled Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run | Fortnite on August 15. Visitors queuing for the attraction at the Orlando and Anaheim parks can accept a mission that awards a Forsworn Trooper Outfit in a new Fortnite adventure called Smugglers Gambit. Disney is an investor in Epic. Previous collaborations were confined to Fortnite seasons and minigames; this is the first extension into the physical parks.
Why This Matters
Sean Shoptaw of Disney Games described the ambition as connecting "stories and worlds across formats into one converged entertainment ecosystem." The operative detail is that the connection was possible because of an engine decision made when the ride was built, not because of a new deal. A production-technology choice turned out to be a distribution asset years later.

That is a live problem for anyone whose compensation is defined per channel. A franchise now earns across theatrical, streaming, parks and a third-party game world at once, and the participation language written for one of those channels captures a shrinking portion of the total.
Specific Implication
Participation and derivative-rights language for franchise properties should be drafted against the ecosystem rather than against a list of named formats. This collaboration was enabled by an engine choice, not a category anyone would have enumerated at signing.

Cineverse Cut Staff In The Quarter Its Revenue Nearly Tripled
Revenue nearly tripled to $30.6 million and the net loss widened to 28 cents a share from 21. The growth and the layoffs came from the same two acquisitions.
CEO Summary
Cineverse disclosed in its fiscal first-quarter earnings on August 13 that it completed a reduction in force after the June 30 quarter end, producing $1.8 million in annual savings. It gave no headcount. The cuts stem from its acquisitions of media services firm Giant Worldwide and ad tech company IndiCue, the same acquisitions that drove the revenue increase. The company is targeting $13 million in annualized cost reductions and synergies, mostly realized by the end of September.
Why This Matters
The revenue that tripled is services and ad tech revenue. The film label sits on top of a business whose growth is coming from selling infrastructure to other people's content. That distinction determines what a distribution deal with Cineverse actually buys.

The slate reflects the same logic. Cineverse is releasing Terrifier installments, Toxic Avenger, Wolf Creek, an Air Bud and a Pan's Labyrinth anniversary re-release. Every one of those is a known title with a pre-existing audience, which is what a company optimizing for predictable marketing spend acquires.
Specific Implication
A filmmaker weighing Cineverse as a distribution home should ask which of the marketing and servicing functions survive the September synergy target. The $13 million reduction runs against $30.6 million of quarterly revenue.
The Facts
  • Reduction in force completed after the June 30 quarter end, worth $1.8 million in annual cost savings. No headcount disclosed. Deadline reports a workforce of 375.
  • A further $4.8 million in cost reductions and synergies identified, bringing the target to $13 million annualized, mostly realized by end of September.
  • Total revenue nearly tripled to $30.6 million, driven by the Giant Worldwide and IndiCue acquisitions. Net loss widened to 28 cents a share from 21 cents a year earlier.
  • As of March 31: 291 full-time employees and nine part-time, on-leave or temporary. 159 in operations, 50 in sales and marketing, 91 in executive, finance, technology and administrative roles. 145 U.S.-based, 155 in India.
  • Formerly Cinedigm, a cinema technology company, re-oriented toward streaming under CEO Chris McGurk, previously head of MGM and Overture Films. Operates AVOD, SVOD and FAST services including Docurama and Fandor, plus the Matchpoint streaming tech platform.
  • Film slate includes the Terrifier franchise, Toxic Avenger, Wolf Creek, an upcoming Air Bud, and a 20th-anniversary re-release of Pan's Labyrinth.
  • Shares rose nearly 5 percent Friday to $3, up more than 30 percent year to date.

Christine Vachon On Financing 'Ratcatcher' In 2026: "We'd Make It For About $300,000"
Asked how a Lynne Ramsay first feature gets financed in America, Vachon said: "What is this public funding of which you speak?" Her number for the same film without it was $300,000.
CEO Summary
At the Edinburgh Film Festival's inaugural UK Film Conference, a panel assessed British classics as if the scripts had just arrived in 2026. The participants were Picturehouse creative director Clare Binns, Killer Films' Christine Vachon, Film4's Stefanie Fahrion, BBC Film's Alice Ojha and Casarotto's Simon Renshaw. Vachon's structural advice on Local Hero was to build with as much soft money as possible, then sell to the U.S. at a high price rather than seek American equity or a pre-buy.
Why This Matters
The panel produced a rare direct comparison of two financing systems applied to the same material. Fahrion noted that voices as distinctive as Ramsay's typically originate with public development or production money in the U.K. Vachon's American answer for the same film was a budget roughly two orders of magnitude smaller.

Her Local Hero structure is the more portable idea. Taking soft money first and selling U.S. rights afterward keeps ownership through the phase where the film is most likely to lose it. A U.S. pre-buy or equity check arrives earlier and costs more of the picture.
Specific Implication
A producer structuring a modestly budgeted feature with U.S. ambitions should sequence soft money ahead of any American equity or pre-buy conversation, per Vachon's stated approach, and treat the U.S. sale as an exit rather than as a financing source.
The Facts
  • Panel hosted by Wendy Mitchell at the inaugural UK Film Conference, Edinburgh Film Festival, August 15, 2026.
  • On Trainspotting: Fahrion cited "shock value" creating a "talking factor" and "FOMO." Renshaw called it "a big swing." Vachon: "I pitch it as genre or genre adjacent," and at the right price "I don't think it's risky at all."
  • On Local Hero, Vachon: "I don't think you get any American equity or a pre-buy unless it was a really big, big star." Her structure: make it "with as much soft money as possible" and then sell it for "a nice high price to the U.S."
  • On Ratcatcher, Renshaw called "that leap from shorts to that first feature" the hurdle, with known cast often crucial to making financiers and distributors comfortable.
  • Vachon on the U.S. equivalent: "What is this public funding of which you speak?" and "We'd make it for about $300,000."
  • On The Wicker Man, Vachon: "exactly what... the A24s, Neons, etc. are looking for right now." Renshaw noted it could be made inexpensively.

The DGA and IATSE put nine conditions on the Warner merger, and they read like a term sheet
The guilds want 15 theatrical films per studio per year, a 45-day PVOD window and 120 days before streaming, which is 30 days longer than what Paramount already promised AMC and Regal.
CEO Summary
The Directors Guild and IATSE wrote to Paramount CEO David Ellison and California Attorney General Rob Bonta late Wednesday urging a settlement of the states' antitrust suit, and attached nine conditions they want secured in a binding agreement. The terms cover output, windows, third-party licensing floors, keeping the two film studios and two TV studios operationally separate, maintaining HBO as a linear channel on third-party platforms, US production quotas, and a commitment that Paramount stays headquartered in Los Angeles. IndieWire assessed each condition against what Paramount has already publicly promised.
Why This Matters
Two of the nine conditions are floors pinned to a five-year average that already contains the post-strike collapse. ProdPro data cited in the reporting shows Paramount shot two features in the United States last year against twelve in 2021, and Warner Bros. five against ten. A US production commitment benchmarked to the 2021-2025 average, excluding 2020 and 2023, therefore ratifies the reduced level rather than restoring the earlier one. The same construction applies to the third-party licensing floors. The guilds have written conditions whose numbers are set by the years they are objecting to.
Specific Implication
The 120-day SVOD window is the term with the widest reach. It exceeds Paramount's existing 90-day commitment to AMC and Regal by 30 days, and at present that length is granted only at the top of the market. If it enters a binding agreement it becomes a slate-wide floor rather than an individually negotiated term.
The Facts
  • The letter was sent late Wednesday to David Ellison and Rob Bonta. It reads: "We cannot overemphasize how damaging the current timeline for the trial ... is to an already struggling industry."
  • Condition 1: Paramount and WBD motion picture studios maintained as separate studios, each keeping its own production, distribution, marketing and exhibition groups as distinct divisions.
  • Condition 2: each studio produces and distributes "a minimum of 15 theatrical films per year with an exclusive theatrical window of at least 45 days (preferably 60 days or more) before PVOD exploitation and 120 days before SVOD exhibition."
  • Condition 3: continued licensing of theatrical films from third parties at no less than the average percentage over the past five years, excluding 2020 and 2023.
  • Condition 4: the same separate operational structure applied to both television studios.
  • Condition 5: HBO maintained as a linear pay television channel available on third-party platforms such as MVPDs and Amazon video.
  • Condition 6: films and television produced in the United States at no less than the five-year average percentage, excluding 2020 and 2023.

Paramount cleared 68 countries today, and now only twelve state AGs stand between it and Warner
Mexico signed off Friday, making 68 national clearances, and Paramount said publicly for the first time that it has "offered commitments and concessions" to the state attorneys general.
CEO Summary
Paramount Skydance announced Friday that Mexico approved its $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, completing regulatory clearance in 68 countries. The antitrust suit brought by 12 state attorneys general, led by California's Rob Bonta, is now the only remaining obstacle to closing. Paramount's own release, posted to its investor site, is headed "PARAMOUNT SKYDANCE SATISFIES ALL REGULATORY CONDITIONS UNDER THE MERGER AGREEMENT TO CLOSE WARNER BROS. DISCOVERY ACQUISITION."
Why This Matters
The most consequential sentence in the release is about cost absorption, not approval. Paramount states it "is required to consider how it can absorb the unnecessary additional financial costs while preserving the longer-term strength of the combined company," and names pension and state retirement funds among the stakeholders it answers to. That is a public accounting of delay tolerance, disclosed while $7 million daily ticking fees begin on Oct. 1 and a trial sits in March. A company that publishes its arithmetic on how long it can wait has narrowed the range within which it can credibly refuse terms.
Specific Implication
The commitments Paramount says it has offered privately are now measurable against the nine conditions the DGA and IATSE published the same day. That comparison narrows the space for a settlement that concedes nothing structural.
The Facts
  • Mexico approved the deal Friday, bringing the total to 68 countries.
  • The lawsuit by 12 state attorneys general is the sole remaining roadblock.

  • Ellison also said: "While we remain confident that the law and the facts are on our side, we have offered commitments and concessions and remain open to working constructively with the state AGs to find a path forward." The content of those commitments has not been disclosed.
  • Company statement: "The unwarranted eight-plus month additional delay for a trial beyond the engagement of the last 9 months will impose needless costs from penalty fees, litigation expenses and business disruption. A budget bill nobody read closely just capped California's $750 million film credit at $5 million a year
SB 122 caps annual credit use at $5 million, so Disney's $45 million California award and Paramount's $37.7 million now pay out over years, and the session ends Aug. 31.
CEO Summary
A California budget trailer bill signed into law June 29 extends caps on the annual use of business tax credits above $5 million and, from 2030, makes permanent a cap of 70 percent of a taxpayer's liability or $5 million, whichever is greater. The film and television credit was not carved out. Entertainment unions have driven roughly 350,000 messages to legislators seeking an exemption, and Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur, who carried the 2025 credit expansion, is working on an amendment before the legislature adjourns Aug. 31.
Why This Matters
Assemblymember Zbur, who carried the bill that created the $750 million program, states plainly that legislators voting on SB 122 believed the film credit was exempt: "As it turns out, the exemption that was in the bill was an exemption only to the refundability aspects of the program, which basically meant that the program was not exempt in the end." An incentive designed over a full session was undone by a drafting distinction in a trailer bill that its own authors misread. The exposure that creates is not political and cannot be argued away, which is why the remedy has to move as legislation inside seventeen days.
Specific Implication
A California credit award and the cash it produces are now different instruments. A $45 million award drawn at $5 million a year is a multi-year receivable, and any production budget treating state credits as near-cash overstates what the project can actually spend.
The Facts
  • SB 122 was signed into law June 29. It extends temporary caps on the use of business tax credits over $5 million in a given tax year and, starting in 2030, enshrines a permanent cap of 70 percent of a taxpayer's liability or $5 million, whichever is greater.
  • Paramount received $37.7 million in the latest California Film Commission round, including for the Viola Davis thriller Ascent and a sequel series to Clueless. Disney received $45 million for an untitled detective series.
  • Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a $420 million boost in 2025, taking the annual program to $750 million and expanding eligibility to half-hour shows, animation and large-scale competition shows.
  • Around 350,000 messages have been sent to legislators by union members, per the Entertainment Union Coalition. The template letter reads: "Budget bill SB 122 puts our program at risk by retroactively changing the rules and threatening the recovery efforts of our already fragile industry throughout California."
  • Brigitta Romanov, president of the California IATSE Council: "Amending SB 122 is essential to helping to ensure that the next production happens in California rather than in the United Kingdom, Australia, Georgia, Vancouver or Saudi Arabia."
  • The legislative session adjourns Aug. 31. A proposed solution is expected within the next week.
  • Nine TV shows were recently awarded $145.5 million to film in California. Los Angeles has not yet seen a significant recovery in production levels since the expanded program was signed.
  • Separately, AB 2319 cleared the Senate Appropriations Committee 5-1 on Thursday. It would create a 35 to 50 percent refundable tax credit for film and TV editing and VFX work, backed by the Motion Picture Editors Guild and the California Post Alliance. It heads to the Senate floor and still requires funding; advocates seek $100 million through a separate budget trailer bill against the same Aug. 31 deadline.
  • AB 2319 was amended in June to require 85 percent of funding go to jobs with above-average industry wages providing pension and health benefits, effectively a union-standards test. The VFX industry is largely non-union. A further amendment Thursday removed a minimum VFX spending requirement, opening it to smaller firms and projects.
  • AB 2403, which would have created a $15 million commercial-production subsidy at 20 to 30 percent of eligible costs, was held in committee and will not advance this year.

CEO Summary
The 12 state attorneys general, the Writers Guild, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery filed a joint case management statement Thursday proposing fact discovery from Aug. 17 to Jan. 8, ahead of the March 2-19 antitrust trial set by Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín. Paramount agreed to pay WBD $7 million for every day the deal does not close after Sept. 30, and the merger agreement expires June 4, 2027 with a $7 billion termination fee attached. The same filing says the parties are working to identify magistrate judges to preside over a settlement conference.
Why This Matters
The disputed trial-day allocation carries the sharpest signal in the filing. The state attorneys general and the Writers Guild are asking for eight of the 12 trial days on the argument that they are litigating two separate cases. If the court accepts that framing, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery are defending two distinct theories of harm on one calendar. A resolution that satisfies the states would not by itself dispose of the guild's claims, which reduces the value of any partial settlement.
Specific Implication
For any deal with a Paramount or Warner Bros. Discovery counterparty, the March 2027 trial date and the June 4, 2027 merger expiration are now fixed reference points. They frame whether the decision-maker on that deal will remain in place through its resolution.
The Facts

  • Fact discovery is proposed to start Aug. 17 and close Jan. 8.
  • U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín set trial for March 2-19, 2027. Final pretrial conference Feb. 24; proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law due April 5.
  • Paramount agreed to pay WBD $7 million for each day the transaction does not close after Sept. 30. Ticking fees would exceed $1 billion by a March trial.
  • The merger agreement expires June 4, 2027, with Paramount on the hook for a $7 billion termination fee.

This merger violates long-standing federal antitrust law. We remain committed to enforcing the law."

Producers are using the Warner fight to push for a streaming-era fin-syn
Producers United wants regulators to mandate that a share of every major platform's programming be licensed from independents with ownership retained, and David Zaslav sold another $22 million in stock this week.
CEO Summary
Producers United, a coalition of career producers, told Puck it is pushing for "fin-syn rewritten for the streaming age," asking regulators to require that a meaningful share of each major platform's programming be commissioned or licensed from independent producers with ownership and profit participation flowing back to creators. The financial interest and syndication rules barred networks from owning what they aired from the 1970s until their repeal in the 1990s. The DGA and IATSE made a narrower version of the same ask in their Wednesday letter to Bonta and Paramount, seeking a guarantee that a combined company keep licensing from outside owners.
Why This Matters
Jeff Sagansky, quoted by name, separates two arguments that the merger fight has fused: "The community is up in arms over how this merger will gut the town in terms of job losses. But job losses are coming whether this merger happens or not." His stated concern is buyer concentration rather than headcount, on the reasoning that "the less the competition, the more pricing power accrues to the streamers, the more control the buyers can exert over the economics vis-à-vis the creative community." Those two problems take different remedies, and blocking a merger addresses only the second. The independent-supply quota is the first proposal on the table aimed at what Sagansky actually describes.
Specific Implication
An independent-production quota with ownership and participation attached would change what backend is negotiated against on platform-commissioned work. The proposal is early and Belloni doubts federal appetite for it, but it is now attached to a named coalition with published language.
The Facts
  • Producers United told Puck: "Opposition to consolidation by itself is not a policy. If regulators will not or cannot keep the studios from owning everything, they must at the very least ensure that the people who make professionally produced content are not written out of it."
  • The group also said: "Fin-syn built and protected America's independent production sector once. Its repeal dismantled it. It is time to write it again for the industry we actually live in, and to return a stake in this business to the people whose work sustains it."
  • Its specific ask is that regulators require a meaningful share of every major platform's programming be commissioned or licensed from independent producers, "with real ownership and profit participation flowing back to the creators who earn it."
  • The fin-syn rules operated from the 1970s into the early 1990s and were repealed during the Clinton administration, after which the industry moved toward vertical integration.
  • The DGA and IATSE letter asked that any settlement include a guarantee that a combined WarnerMount continue to license theatrical films and content on linear and streaming platforms from outside owners.
  • Belloni's market-share figures: WarnerMount generated 22 percent of the US box office for all wide-release films over the past two years, including A24, Lionsgate and Amazon MGM in the denominator. In television it would account for roughly 20 percent of domestic watch time excluding YouTube. In US streaming alone, the Paramount and WBD services generated 3.8 percent of viewing in May per Nielsen, fifth place.
  • David Zaslav sold a further $22 million in WBD stock this week, bringing the total to nearly $200 million since the Paramount deal was announced.
  • WBD streaming revenue passed $3.1 billion last quarter for the first time, up 10 percent year over year.
  • Cinema United's late-September Fall Summit schedule excludes Paramount, which had been on the tour in prior years. AMC and Regal endorsed the merger; Cinema United remains opposed.
  • Two Paramount executives told Belloni they would quit rather than relocate out of California.
  • Paramount is planning thousands of layoffs if the merger closes. Belloni's sources say creative development and production staff would not relocate, while the C-suite, finance, administration, streaming management and ad sales could.
  • Disclosures carried in the piece: RedBird Capital is an investor in Puck, and Zaslav is a de minimis investor.

The term compression on the cable side is the tell. Rights holders should expect cable license terms to keep shortening regardless of how a title rates.

On a catalog title with global reach, rights holders licensing a worldwide grant should price territory and term as separate negotiating points rather than a single package. YouTube just doubled the bar to get paid, and the people it lets in are the ones with track records
From February, YouTube Partner Program entry requires 8,000 watch hours over 12 months or 20 million Shorts views in 90 days, double the current thresholds.
CEO Summary
YouTube announced this week the largest change to its monetization policy in nearly a decade, doubling the thresholds for acceptance into the YouTube Partner Program beginning in February. Google chief business officer Philipp Schindler said on the most recent earnings call that YouTube's subscription business, driven by Music and Premium, is growing faster than advertising. Reuters Institute data cited in the piece shows more people now watch online news video than broadcast or cable news for the first time since tracking began.
Why This Matters
Schindler's statement that subscription revenue is outgrowing advertising sits underneath the threshold change and explains it. A platform whose growth comes from Premium and Music is not optimizing for impression volume, and the content that justifies a subscription is not the content that maximizes ad-supported views. Raising the entry bar removes supply that serves the older model. Digital media strategist Ruben Ceuppens reads the same move from the advertiser side, noting that it narrows the monetized pool "to those with a longer track record."
Specific Implication
Independent distribution is frequently used as leverage against a traditional platform deal. The entry cost of that alternative doubles in February, which raises the value of an audience a creator already has and lowers the credibility of one they intend to build.
The Facts
  • Beginning in February, creators must reach 8,000 watch hours over 12 months, or 20 million Shorts views within 90 days, to be accepted into the YouTube Partner Program. Both thresholds are double the current ones.
  • Ruben Ceuppens on LinkedIn: "advertisers increasingly want predictability: known creators, established patterns, [and] lower risk of controversy blindsiding a campaign. ... By raising the bar to qualify for ad revenue, YouTube is effectively narrowing its pool of monetized creators to those with a longer track record."
  • Philipp Schindler, Google chief business officer, on the most recent earnings call: "YouTube subscription business, which thrives across living room screens, is growing faster than ads, particularly driven by YouTube Music and Premium."
  • Reuters Institute data: more than 75 percent of people now watch news via online sources such as YouTube. For the first time since Reuters began tracking, more people watch online news videos than broadcast or cable news. YouTube accounts for nearly 35 percent of survey respondents' news diets, second behind Facebook at 43 percent.
  • Video news consumption on traditional sites fell five percentage points between 2023 and 2026 to under 25 percent, while consumption on video platforms including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram grew by a combined 17 percentage points.

  • YouTube's news partnerships director is Brandon Feldman. The platform has promoted journalists who left legacy newsrooms, including former CNN anchor Don Lemon.

  • Prior moves in the same direction cited: YouTube's Alex Cooper partnership and its recent Peacock deal.

Selena Gomez is being sued over what "head of marketing" was supposed to mean
Investors who put nearly $1.2 million into Wondermind sued Selena Gomez in Delaware federal court Thursday, and one securities fraud claim rests on the promise she would be "intimately involved."
CEO Summary
Two investor entities sued Selena Gomez, her mother Mandy Teefey and co-founder Daniella Pierson on Aug. 13 in Delaware federal court, alleging securities fraud, fraudulent inducement and breach of contract at the collapsed mental health company Wondermind. The complaint says the app was never built, the JP Morgan and Fidelity partnerships pitched to investors did not exist, and nobody told investors for three years. Among the alleged misrepresentations: that Gomez would be "intimately involved" and would serve as head of marketing. Gomez and Teefey had previously put $8 million of their own money into the company.
Why This Matters
The complaint's timeline is its notable feature: it alleges the defendants continued to misrepresent the company's health as recently as April 2026, nearly a year after Forbes reported the missed payroll and layoffs. Pleading misrepresentation past the point of public distress reporting extends the founders' claimed exposure across the company's entire life rather than the original raise alone. It converts routine investor reassurance during a wind-down into alleged securities conduct.
Specific Implication
Talent taking a named operating title, such as head of marketing, in a company raising outside capital should confirm that fundraising materials describing the role match a documented, defined commitment. The complaint treats that description as a securities representation rather than a promotional credit.
The Facts
  • Two investor entities, Wondermind SRS 44 and Bespoke Wondermind SPV, sued Selena Gomez, her mother Mandy Teefey and co-founder Daniella Pierson in Delaware federal court on Thursday, Aug. 13, alleging securities fraud, fraudulent inducement and breach of contract.
  • The plaintiffs say they invested nearly $1.2 million.
  • The securities fraud claim alleges misrepresentations including that Gomez would be "intimately involved" in the company and overstatement of her level of involvement as the company's "head of marketing." Other alleged misrepresentations: Pierson's business acumen, Teefey's fitness to lead, and the company's growth trajectory.
  • From the complaint: "The partnerships did not exist. The initiatives never materialized. The app was never built. And for three years, while the Company quietly collapsed around them, not one of its founders, officers, or directors said a word to the investors whose money was funding the collapse."
  • The suit alleges that in a May 2022 meeting and June 2022 emails, Pierson said Wondermind had already secured partnerships with JP Morgan and Fidelity, expected $5 million in ad revenue that year, and had 150,000 subscribers, and sent a document suggesting the valuation could eventually surpass $4 billion.
  • Wondermind launched in 2022. Forbes reported in May 2025 that it had run out of cash and missed payroll; days later, that it had laid off nearly two-thirds of staff. A September 2025 article in The Cut alleged erratic behavior by Teefey (which she denied) and reported that Teefey and Gomez had put $8 million of their own money into the company.
  • The suit alleges the defendants continued to misrepresent the company's health as recently as April 2026.
  • Pierson alone also faces claims of conversion and unjust enrichment for allegedly using investor funds for personal expenses.

A judge says a Hollywood litigator may have directed the smear sites

CEO Summary
Los Angeles Superior Court judge Michael Whitaker denied Bryan Freedman's motion to dismiss Alexa Nikolas's defamation case on Wednesday, finding she established a probability of prevailing. The connections surfaced through the It Ends With Us litigation and a sister suit by publicist Stephanie Jones. Freedman has previously denied involvement and did not respond to a request for comment.

The ruling's force is in what survived the opinion defense. The court found the site's allegations "all imply provably false assertions of fact." It also credited a cybersecurity expert's report from the related Stephanie Jones suit linking the site about Nikolas to sites targeting other women, including Amanda Ghost. Crediting cross-case forensic linkage at this stage moves anonymous-site attribution from reputational suspicion into triable territory for the attorney himself, not only the publicists and operatives who build such sites.
Specific Implication
Individuals or their representatives evaluating an anonymous negative site that appeared during a dispute now have a forensic precedent, established in this ruling, for pursuing discovery on common authorship across similar sites.
The Facts

  • The court found the site's allegations "all imply provably false assertions of fact" that Nikolas is "either a criminal who has committed criminal acts, or she is not," rejecting Freedman's opinion defense.

  • The connection surfaced through the It Ends With Us litigation, in which Blake Lively accused Justin Baldoni and his PR team, crisis publicist Melissa Nathan and digital operative Jed Wallace, of running a smear machine. A sister suit by publicist Stephanie Jones alleged Nathan and Wallace have long created smear sites targeting women.

The Top House Judiciary Democrat Gave David Ellison Until August 26 to Sit for a Transcribed Interview
Raskin says he has sent Ellison four letters in 12 months and gotten no reply to any of them, and the same day, Paramount confirmed it has discussed creating an editorial board for CNN.
CEO Summary
Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, wrote to Paramount CEO David Ellison inviting him to a transcribed interview about the Warner Bros. Discovery merger and gave him until August 26 to schedule it. The letter accuses Ellison of "colluding with President Trump and his administration to curtail media independence," citing changes at CBS News and a December Wall Street Journal report that he assured administration officials he would make sweeping changes to CNN. Hours later the Journal reported Paramount has discussed creating an editorial board for CNN once the merger closes.
Why This Matters
Raskin, as a member of the House minority, has no power to compel Ellison's testimony; his letter is his fourth in 12 months and Ellison has not responded to any of them. Paramount confirmed the same day that it has discussed an editorial board for CNN, a step Bonta has not requested. Bonta, who leads the 12-state antitrust suit, has said publicly that CNN was not the basis for his suit and that a settlement requires structural remedies. An editorial board is a governance measure, not a structural remedy of the kind Bonta has said he wants.

Paramount's own chief legal officer, Makan Delrahim, characterized the congressional letter as unfounded ("there is no corruption here") while saying the company would engage with Raskin. A similar newsroom-governance commitment was made during approval of Skydance's original Paramount deal, when the company created an ombudsman role for the news division and filled it with Kenneth Weinstein, formerly of the Hudson Institute.
The Facts
  • Deadline for Ellison to schedule: August 26. Raskin has sent four letters over 12 months; Ellison has answered none.

  • Paramount statement: "We always remain open to internal improvements to journalistic integrity. However, as we have maintained, using state powers to try to control speech would threaten the protections guaranteed by the First Amendment."
  • Chief legal officer Makan Delrahim, at a Politico event Tuesday: "You can allege all you want. There is no corruption here." He said Paramount would be "happy to engage with" Raskin.
  • Bonta leads 12 state attorneys general challenging the merger and has said a settlement requires structural remedies.
  • Ellison published a New York Times op-ed last week arguing the opposition is driven by CNN.

Between April and last month, Netflix (Clips), Prime Video (Clips), Peacock, Disney+ (Verts), Paramount+ and HBO Max (Shorts) each launched a vertical short-form feed inside their mobile apps. A clip seeded on social platforms functions as marketing, while the same AI-segmented scene served in-app as programming is direct exploitation of the underlying series. That shifts scene-level excerpting from the promotional side of the ledger to the licensed side.

CEO Summary
The DGA and IATSE sent a joint letter Wednesday to California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Paramount CEO David Ellison urging a settlement of the antitrust suit against the $110 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger, or at minimum an expedited trial. Their conditions: keep the film studios separate, commit to 45-day theatrical windows, maintain the promise of 30 films a year. That puts them opposite the Writers Guild, which supports the states' suit and has filed its own to block the deal. Bonta's office responded Thursday and did not move, saying the merger "violates long-standing federal antitrust law." Trial is set for 12 days, March 2 to March 15, 2027.
Why This Matters
The split tracks what each union sells. IATSE and DGA members earn when production volume exists, so a stalled deal holding projects in limbo is itself the injury. The WGA's own filing locates the harm in buyer concentration, arguing the merger "would eliminate competition for buying film and television writing." A union whose damage is measured in idle months has an interest in speed on almost any terms; a union whose damage is a permanently smaller buyer market has an interest in blocking regardless of timeline. SAG-AFTRA's position, supporting the suit while naming settlement safeguards it would accept, sits between the two because its members carry both exposures.
Specific Implication
Two major crafts unions have now put specific settlement terms in writing as conditions they would accept: separate studios, 45-day windows, and a 30-film annual commitment. That sets a concrete reference point for anyone modeling a negotiated outcome to the case.

  • IATSE reports member hours worked in 2025 were down nearly 36 percent from 2022. The DGA has seen a 40 percent decrease in employment since 2022, per a union source.
