  • Settlement conditions sought: separate film studios, 45-day theatrical windows, 30 films per year.
  • Bonta's office, Thursday: "the proposed Warner Bros./Paramount merger will mean higher costs, less competition, lower wages, job cuts and fewer movies and TV shows. This merger violates long-standing federal antitrust law. We remain committed to enforcing the law."
  • The WGA supports the states' suit and filed its own, arguing the merger "would eliminate competition for buying film and television writing, resulting in suppressed compensation, worse deal terms, and reduced programming volume and diversity."
  • SAG-AFTRA supports the suit but would accept a settlement with "enforceable safeguards against reduced production by the studios with guarantees of increases in the percentage of productions made in the USA."
  • Teamsters motion picture division head Lindsay Dougherty: "Touting worker prosperity, without commitments, while simultaneously threatening their livelihood in the press as a bargaining chip begs the question, what is in this deal for American film and television workers?"
  • Trial: 12 days, March 2 to March 15, 2027, before U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín. Xavier Becerra, Democratic nominee for California governor, urged settlement Tuesday.

The inventory available to order, air and generate residuals from entertainment programming is being reset by contract for the life of the rights deals, not rationed year to year by programming judgment.
Specific Implication
Any long-dated deal valued on network exhibition should be priced against an 11-year contractual reduction in broadcast entertainment inventory, not a single-season fluctuation.

Two Hollywood Unions Break With the WGA and Ask California to Let the Paramount-Warner Merger Through
The unions asked for a 45-day theatrical window and said they would prefer 60 or more, plus a 120-day streaming holdback and Paramount's headquarters kept in Los Angeles, one day after David Ellison threatened to leave the state.
CEO Summary
The Directors Guild of America and IATSE jointly wrote to California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison on Wednesday, urging them to settle the antitrust suit over the $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery merger on conditions rather than fight to a March 2, 2027 trial. The letter puts both unions at odds with the Writers Guild, which sued to block the deal. It sets out nine conditions, including keeping the two studios operationally separate, minimum theatrical output with a 45-day exclusive window, and keeping Paramount headquartered in Los Angeles.
Why This Matters
The letter's substance is a behavioral consent decree, the category of remedy Bonta has publicly ruled out, so its practical function is pressure rather than a settlement blueprint. It aligns two guilds with Paramount's timing problem without endorsing the deal. Its fallback request for an earlier trial date targets the delay itself, the variable the unions say is already costing their members work. A regulator holding out for structural relief now faces labor on the other side of the courtroom aisle. That changes the political cost of running the clock to trial even if it changes nothing in the legal posture.
Specific Implication
The 45-to-60-day theatrical window figure in the unions' letter gives any negotiation over exclusivity terms a specific number to cite. It was offered to win labor support during a contested merger process rather than negotiated as a standalone distribution term. Its durability depends on a settlement Bonta has indicated he is not inclined to accept.
The Facts
  • The letter was signed by DGA national executive director Russell Hollander and IATSE international president Matthew Loeb, and sent to Bonta and Paramount leadership on Wednesday.
  • The Writers Guild filed its own antitrust suit to block the merger.
  • Nine conditions, per TheWrap. The most prominent: Paramount and Warner Bros. maintained as separate studios with their own distribution, marketing and production divisions; Paramount's headquarters kept in Los Angeles. Others as written: each studio produces and distributes a minimum of 15 theatrical films per year with an exclusive theatrical window of at least 45 days, preferably 60 or more, before PVOD and 120 days before SVOD; third-party theatrical licensing held at no less than the five-year average percentage, excluding 2020 and 2023; the same separate structure for the television studios; HBO maintained as a linear pay-television channel available on third-party platforms; US production held at no less than the five-year average; third-party original-content licensing held at no less than the five-year average.
  • From the letter: "While we have been consistent in our view that mergers, such as this one, historically offer few benefits to workers, we are also particularly concerned about the negative impact a delay in the decision regarding the proposed merger will have on our members and the industry at large." And: "We are aware of productions that have been put on hold or canceled altogether."
  • Bonta led a 12-state coalition suing in July over consolidation in basic cable and theatrical distribution. Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin issued a temporary restraining order and set trial for March 2, 2027. Paramount had sought November; Bonta asked for April 2027.
  • Bonta has said he is not interested in behavioral remedies, including a 30-films-a-year pledge with a 45-day window, and will only accept structural remedies.
  • Exhibition is split: AMC's Adam Aron and Regal's Eduardo Acuna have endorsed the merger; the trade group Cinema United opposes it; Cinemark's Sean Gamble has not endorsed. More than 90% of Cinema United members operate fewer than 75 screens. Cinema United has balked at Paramount's three-year exhibitor contracts, pushing for a longer commitment.
  • Per LightShed: the merger agreement expires June 4, 2027; a loss would trigger a $7 billion breakup fee, which the firm calls the largest in US corporate history; Paramount's 30-film pledge was first put to Bonta's office in May inside a 12-point behavioral consent decree that went unanswered; Bloomberg reported three-year contracts with AMC and Regal guaranteeing 30 films a year, a 45-day minimum window and a 90-day streaming holdback on close.
  • The combined company is expected to carry a debt load of roughly $79 billion to $80 billion.
  • If no settlement is reached, the unions ask both sides to agree to an earlier trial date.

Brands Are Hiring Hollywood as the Production Sector Sheds 49,000 Jobs
Motion picture and video production has shed 49,000 jobs in a decade, down 21 percent, while brand-funded projects now run from tens of thousands of dollars to north of $50 million.
CEO Summary
Major consumer brands are building in-house studios and hiring Hollywood executives to run them, with Gap bringing in former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman as chief entertainment officer and Procter & Gamble, Starbucks, Kraft Heinz, Dick's Sporting Goods and e.l.f. all launching entertainment arms. Budgets for these projects run from tens of thousands of dollars for a raw digital series to more than $50 million for a campaign built around the Super Bowl or World Cup. The shift is happening as the production sector contracts: Bureau of Labor Statistics figures show companies in motion picture and video production have cut 49,000 jobs over the past decade, a 21 percent decline, and Luminate data shows the industry is producing nearly 50 percent fewer TV shows than it did before the 2023 strikes.
Why This Matters
The structural change is in who originates. Toyota conceiving a talk show and pitching it to creator Kareem Rahma reverses the customary direction of the pitch. The executive hires show brands acquiring the commissioning function itself rather than renting production capacity project by project. That makes these companies buyers in the development market, competing for the same executives, filmmakers and formats as studios, at the moment studio commissioning is shrinking, rather than advertisers purchasing finished access to talent.
The Facts
  • Companies in motion picture and video production have shed 49,000 jobs in the past decade, a 21 percent decline, per US Bureau of Labor Statistics figures cited by THR. Peak sector employment was about 289,000; recent levels are roughly 100,000 below the October 2022 high.

YouTube Doubles the Bar to Start Earning Money

YouTube announced on August 10 that new applicants to its Partner Program will need 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year or 20 million qualified Shorts views over the past 90 days, double the current 4,000 hours and 10 million views. It lands in the same week X restricted creator payouts to original content and Meta is spending to lure creators away. A platform tightening terms while its rivals loosen theirs is making a statement about relative position: YouTube is pricing its distribution as scarce, and the value of an already-monetized channel rises accordingly.

For a creator or business relying on Shorts Creators Pool revenue, that income should be modeled as conditional on maintaining 10 million qualified views every 90 days. It is not a fixed, guaranteed line once initial eligibility is reached.

  • New YPP thresholds effective February 1, 2027: 8,000 qualified watch hours over the previous 365 days, or 20 million qualified Shorts views over the previous 90 days. Current thresholds are 4,000 watch hours or 10 million Shorts views. The 1,000-subscriber requirement is unchanged.

Streaming Took More Upfront Money Than Broadcast and Cable Combined, and Every CPM Still Fell
Streaming upfront commitments rose 30 percent to $17.2 billion against $8.63 billion for broadcast and just under $8 billion for cable, and CPMs fell in all three: broadcast 4.2 percent, cable 8.5 percent, streaming 4.9 percent.
CEO Summary
Advertisers committed about $33.8 billion in the 2026 primetime upfront, up 9.1 percent, according to Media Dynamics Inc. Streaming commitments rose 30 percent to roughly $17.2 billion from $13.2 billion, while broadcast fell 5.3 percent to $8.63 billion and cable fell 7.7 percent to just under $8 billion, the fourth consecutive year of declines for both. Cost per thousand viewers dropped across every category: broadcast down 4.2 percent to $41.65, cable down 8.5 percent to $17.70, and streaming down 4.9 percent to $25.90.
Why This Matters
Streaming upfront commitments rose 30 percent to about $17.2 billion in the 2026 primetime cycle, more than broadcast ($8.63 billion) and cable (just under $8 billion) combined, per Media Dynamics Inc. figures reported by Variety. Streaming's cost per thousand viewers fell 4.9 percent over the same period, while broadcast CPM fell 4.2 percent and cable CPM fell 8.5 percent. Dollar growth in streaming therefore came from higher volume of inventory sold rather than from higher per-viewer pricing. Broadcast and cable commitments both declined for a fourth consecutive year.

Most sellers cited by Variety, including Fox, Paramount Skydance and Disney, reported gains in percentage terms rather than dollar figures; Netflix stated it "nearly doubled" its ad commitments without disclosing the prior-year dollar base for that figure.
Specific Implication
A multi-year output or ad-inventory commitment tied to broadcast or cable network performance should account for the CPM declines of 4.2 percent (broadcast) and 8.5 percent (cable) recorded in this cycle. Both categories are in their fourth consecutive year of decline.

A Combined Warner-Paramount Would Still Earn Most of Its Profit From Linear TV
Linear produced $2.5 billion of adjusted EBITDA on revenue down 14 percent, while the combined studio business earned $132 million, down 84 percent, on revenue down 26 percent.
CEO Summary
Combining the just-reported Q2 numbers from Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery produces a pro-forma view of the merged company. Revenue would have been $15.6 billion, down 6.2 percent year over year, with net profit of $190 million, adjusted EBITDA of $2.98 billion, up 5.8 percent, and free cash flow of $830 million, essentially flat. Linear television would have supplied about 46 percent of revenue at $7.12 billion, down 14 percent, but $2.5 billion of adjusted EBITDA, up 3.5 percent. Streaming revenue would have been $5.55 billion, up 10 percent, with $878 million of adjusted EBITDA, up 60 percent. The studio business would have been the weak leg: $3.64 billion of revenue, down 26 percent, and $132 million of adjusted EBITDA, down 84 percent.
Why This Matters
The pro-forma exposes the merger's central structural bind. The segment generating most of the combined profit is the same declining asset regulators are most likely to demand the merged company address. Management's promise to bring leverage down within three years of closing depends on exactly that cash flow. A structural remedy would not merely shrink the company; it would strip the earnings that make the debt serviceable. That is why the remedies fight is existential for the capital structure rather than a negotiation over conditions. It is also why the studio segment's collapse matters: it removes the alternative profit engine that would make a linear divestiture survivable.
Specific Implication
An output commitment or overall deal negotiated against either studio currently sits against a company whose studio segment, by this pro-forma measure, contributed a small and declining share of adjusted EBITDA relative to linear television.
The Facts
  • Pro-forma combined Q2 2026 (PSKY plus WBD, no combined earnings call): revenue $15.6 billion, down 6.2 percent; net profit $190 million; adjusted EBITDA $2.98 billion, up 5.8 percent; free cash flow $830 million, up $14 million.
  • Linear TV: about 46 percent of total revenue. Revenue $7.12 billion, down 14 percent. Adjusted EBITDA $2.5 billion, up 3.5 percent.
  • Streaming: about 36 percent of total revenue. Revenue $5.55 billion, up 10 percent. Adjusted EBITDA $878 million, up 60 percent.
  • Studios: about 23 percent of total revenue. Revenue $3.64 billion, down 26 percent. Adjusted EBITDA $132 million, down 84 percent.
  • Percentages do not total 100 because internal licensing revenue and corporate costs are deducted.
  • Reporting caveat: Paramount books its CBS Media Ventures syndication arm inside linear TV, while Warner books syndication inside its studio business.
  • Q2 comparisons absorb the loss of the NBA in its largest annual revenue quarter and no Final Four for CBS.
  • Warner and Paramount collectively wrote off $15 billion from the value of the cable business in 2024.

  • Management has promised Wall Street it will bring leverage down to reasonable levels within three years of closing.

ByteDance's New Model Blocks 80 Percent of Copyright Prompts After Hollywood Complained
Seedance 2.5 blocked 80 percent of copyright prompts and 100 percent of attempts to generate video from copyrighted images, but it blocked them at the output stage after rendering, and it still produced Shark Tale's Oscar unprompted by name.
CEO Summary
ByteDance's new video generator Seedance 2.5 is successfully blocking most attempts to reproduce Hollywood intellectual property, according to research shared with Deadline by VN.ai, a startup that stress tests generative AI tools for copyright infringement. The predecessor model, Seedance 2.0, produced a wave of infringing videos including a viral Tom Cruise and Brad Pitt fight clip and drew cease-and-desist letters from Disney and Netflix over titles including Stranger Things and The Avengers. VN.ai found Seedance 2.5 blocks around 80 percent of prompts involving copyrighted material and 100 percent of attempts to create video from copyrighted images, but does so by moderating the rendered output rather than refusing the prompt.
Why This Matters
Because the blocking happens only after a faithful render, the improvement is evidence for the studios' core claim, not against it. The protected works remain in the model, and what changed is ByteDance's willingness to serve them. That leaves the training-data cause of action, the basis of rightsholder leverage, fully intact while removing the viral outputs that generated public pressure. It is a compliance posture that lowers ByteDance's visibility as a defendant without lowering its exposure.
Specific Implication
For a rights holder pursuing enforcement against AI-generated reproductions of well-known characters, VN.ai's findings indicate that output-stage detection is currently more consistent for famous IP than for lesser-known characters. Prompt variations were still shown to bypass the guardrail on the latter.
The Facts
  • Seedance 2.5 launched in late July 2026. VN.ai stress tested it and shared findings with Deadline.
  • VN.ai found Seedance 2.5 blocks around 80 percent of prompts involving copyrighted material, described as far more consistent than Seedance 2.0 or the Seedream 5 image generator, and 100 percent of attempts to create videos from copyrighted images.
  • The block happens at the output stage: the model renders the video, moderates it, and refuses to serve it.
  • VN.ai produced a faithful video of Shark Tale's Oscar without using the character's name or the DreamWorks title.
  • Seedance 2.0 produced a viral Tom Cruise versus Brad Pitt fight video and reproductions of titles including Stranger Things and The Avengers; Disney and Netflix sent ByteDance cease-and-desist letters, and ByteDance said it had "heard the concerns."
  • ByteDance spokesperson: "ByteDance launches models with AI transparency measures and guardrails designed to prevent the unauthorized use of intellectual property, which we continually work to strengthen in collaboration with creative communities as AI technologies evolve."
  • Deadline reported last week that MiniMax H3, another Chinese model, was being used to create remixed videos of The Office, Friends and Star Wars; MiniMax did not respond to a request for comment.
  • In the same reporting, VN.ai generated bootleg images of Elsa, Shrek and Buzz Lightyear via Seedream 5.0 through a third-party API, and found that tweaking prompts to specify exact pixel sizes defeated character-name denials.

Spotify Put a Ringer Podcast on Amazon's Twitch to Slow YouTube
The first broadcast drew 670 viewers on a platform with 150 million monthly visitors, against YouTube's 2.5 billion, and the show still posts to YouTube and Spotify the same day.
CEO Summary
Spotify-owned The Ringer began live-streaming its sports gambling show Ringer Wise Guys on Amazon-owned Twitch on Monday, its first video podcast on the platform and the first activity on a Ringer Twitch account dormant for roughly eight years. Episodes still post to YouTube, Spotify and other feeds later the same day, so only the live window moved. Twitch has 150 million average monthly visitors against YouTube's more than 2.5 billion monthly active users, and its entire Talk Shows and Podcasts category accounted for under 1% of live viewers on the morning of publication.
Why This Matters
Dan Clancy's on-record sorting of formats defines the actual contested ground: shows that riff and respond suit Twitch, and guest-driven interview shows do not. Twitch is not bidding for podcasting's on-demand catalog but for the live premiere hour of a specific interactive subset. That narrows the challenge to YouTube while making it more precise, since the premiere is where chat, polls and live monetization operate. It is the one piece of an established show a rival platform can take without asking the audience to move its library habits.
Specific Implication
Splitting a live premiere window from same-day on-demand distribution, as done here, creates two distribution rights that can be licensed to different platforms rather than one. The audience scale on the live side here, 670 viewers, is a fraction of the show's existing on-demand reach.
The Facts

  • Twitch has 150 million average monthly visitors; YouTube has well over 2.5 billion monthly active users. Twitch's Talk Shows and Podcasts category accounted for less than 1% of all live viewers on the morning of publication and has 3.6 million followers, against 53.1 million for the Just Chatting category.
  • Nearly 70% of Twitch viewers are between 18 and 34.
  • Noah Malale, Spotify's director of originals partnerships and new initiatives: "We always have wanted to meet fans where they are. Bill and The Ringer have always wanted to be on the forefront of new media." And: "We want to definitely lean into what makes Twitch Twitch."
  • Twitch CEO Dan Clancy: "It's not that every podcast is necessarily right for Twitch," citing interview shows where a guest wants a controlled environment. "But there are other podcasts, and the Wise Guys is a perfect example, where they are riffing and they're responding and they're adapting." He likens the interactivity to "the age-old radio call-in show."
  • Wise Guys, rebranded from The Ringer Gambling Show ahead of the move, streams Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday, with episodes posted later the same day to YouTube, Spotify and other podcast platforms. The first broadcast ran a Twitch Poll on an NFL division race.

"Lanterns" premieres Sunday on HBO after a nearly seven-year path involving at least four takes and two creative teams, the first live-action scripted DC series developed under James Gunn and Peter Safran. DC and HBO also passed on Poison Ivy and Catwoman pitches, and "Booster Gold" is searching for a new writer. Why This Matters
The pattern locates DC's television problem in governance rather than economics. The regime whose first move was to cancel the five series it inherited has now killed or stalled most of the slate it announced to replace them. The 2023 reset installed a taste bottleneck where a pipeline was promised. A label that discards a fully scripted season over a creative disagreement, with cost never raised, is exercising a veto that operates after delivery. That is the stage at which it is most expensive for every party involved.
Specific Implication
An overall or series commitment tied to franchise television at a major superhero label carries a reported risk of extended, multi-regime development delay or cancellation independent of budget. Both the WBD and Disney examples in this reporting show that risk.

And: "It wasn't a note that was borne or driven by budget. No one ever said, 'Listen, we can't afford to make the version of the show you're talking about.' I never got that note."

David Ellison told Paramount's 12-member Executive Leadership Team last Wednesday that he will move the company to Tennessee, Texas, Georgia or another state if California Attorney General Rob Bonta does not negotiate a settlement in the 12-state antitrust suit against the $110 billion Warner Bros. Discovery acquisition. He set an October 1 deadline, the date a $7 million-per-day ticking fee to WBD shareholders begins, and said the board has already approved the move. Bonta Names His Price: Structure Yes, a 30-Film Promise No
Bonta called Ellison's 30-films-a-year pledge "an old stale promise," ruled out a CNN divestiture, and said only separating corporate entities settles it. Hours later Paramount's legal chief said everything is on the table.
CEO Summary
California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Tuesday he would consider structural remedies to settle the 12-state antitrust suit against Paramount Skydance's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, defining them as "keeping certain corporate entities separate" in the challenged markets. He rejected behavioral remedies including David Ellison's pledge of 30 films a year, calling it "an old stale promise," and separately ruled out a CNN divestiture on the grounds that the complaint has "little, if any, mention of CNN." Hours later at the same Politico conference, Paramount Chief Legal Officer Makan Delrahim said "everything is on the table" while predicting the states' cable claim "will fall apart because of the market definition."
Why This Matters
The consequential move is the CNN carve-out. By taking the one politically convenient divestiture off the table while insisting on structural relief, Bonta narrowed the settlement space to the assets covered by the three markets the complaint pleads. That points any remedy at studio output or basic cable channels. Those are the assets the merger exists to combine, so the settlement Bonta says he will accept is priced close to the cost of not merging at all.
Specific Implication
An output commitment a studio puts in writing to an exhibitor or regulator carries weight only to the extent the relevant enforcer classifies it as structural rather than behavioral. Bonta's rejection of the 30-film pledge is the on-record test of that distinction.
The Facts
  • Bonta spoke at Politico's California Agenda conference in Sacramento. He leads 12 states in the suit, filed last month.
  • The complaint alleges harm in three markets: wide-release theatrical film distribution, anticipated big-budget blockbusters, and basic cable channel licensing.
  • On settlement: "I think they're eager to enter those talks. And we are very happy with where we are. Literally, on in every development in this case, we have won and they have lost."
  • On Ellison's framing of the suit as political: "What Mr. Ellison has posited is false. Yesterday, false. Today, false. Tomorrow, false."
  • Delrahim on the relocation threat: "I heard the attorney general say that this was some kind of blackmail attempt for the lawsuit. It is not." He noted the merger has been approved in roughly 67 countries.
  • Delrahim said he takes Bonta "at his word" that the case is not about CNN.
  • Bonta declined to comment on a Wall Street Journal report that Governor Gavin Newsom had urged him to settle.
  • The Writers Guild of America said Ellison's exit threat "proves the danger of its outsized power."

China Made 128,000 Microdramas in One Quarter and 95 Percent Were AI
AI "digital human" titles went from 7 to 38 percent of China's top 100 short dramas in a year. Zhang Xiaolei did 200 microdramas in two years, has had one booking in 2026, and now farms chilies.
CEO Summary
China released about 128,000 new microdramas in the first quarter of 2026, more than 95 percent of them AI productions, according to Caixin. AI-driven "digital human" dramas rose from 7 percent to 38 percent of the top 100 manju titles in twelve months, per DataEye, and those 100 titles drew 2.55 billion views. An AI series costs $14,000 to $28,000 against over $100,000 for comparable live action, with the cheapest productions now under $2,800, and production teams have compressed from six people to one.
Why This Matters
The structural feature beneath the cost collapse is vertical integration. ByteDance owns the production software, the distribution app, and the ad network, so the margin removed from performers and crews is recaptured inside a single company's stack. That same company acts as the de facto enforcer against unauthorized likeness use. A market in which the chief beneficiary of synthetic supply also adjudicates misuse of real faces leaves performers without an independent enforcement layer, which matters more to likeness-deal risk than the per-episode rate.
Specific Implication
The $15-to-$74-per-episode licensing rate reported here applies to volume-tier microdrama production. Actors and representatives negotiating likeness rights in that specific bulk-licensing tier should treat this as the current comp for that tier only, not as a benchmark for prestige-format deals.

Why This Matters
The load-bearing element in Shapiro's history is the blackout-era mechanism: the side without the consumer relationship blinked first. Leverage belongs to whoever sits at the moment of choice, not to whoever owns the pipe or the library. Run forward, that mechanism puts the decade's platform winners in the losing seat if an agent layer forms above them. That leaves Netflix and YouTube in the structural position cable occupied when carriage standoffs began going against it.

Earnings correlate more strongly with follower count and views than with engagement metrics, contradicting a year of industry guidance. The line that reorders the category is that creators above $250,000 report building structurally different businesses from those under $10,000. Averages drawn across that split describe nobody, and the brand-launch wave reads as the lower tier attempting to cross into the top tier's business model, not as expansion of a healthy middle.
Specific Implication
The survey's own split runs TikTok for near-term branded-content volume and performance, and Instagram as the platform higher-earning creators cite as sustaining a durable business. That distinction, not interchangeability, is what a creator deal or platform-exclusivity negotiation should be built around.

California AG Rob Bonta Says a Merged Paramount-Warner Would Leave Four Distributors Controlling Over 90% of Anticipated Blockbusters
Bonta names three markets, not CNN or streaming: wide-release distribution, blockbuster distribution and cable. He says the merged company would hold nearly a third of theatrical distribution and 50 of the most popular cable channels.
CEO Summary
California Attorney General Rob Bonta published a guest column in Deadline laying out the twelve states' antitrust case against Paramount Skydance's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which goes to a two-week trial in March 2027. He argues the merger creates illegal concentration in three markets and would leave four distributors controlling more than 90% of anticipated blockbusters, which account for 88% of box office revenue over the past four years. He explicitly rejects the concessions Paramount has been offering: the harm "can't be remedied with a few one-off, piecemeal promises."
Why This Matters
The procedural detail carries the leverage read. Both companies agreed to pause the merger rather than contest preliminary injunction hearings, which handed the states a trial calendar without forcing them to prove likelihood of success first. A defendant confident that the blockbuster-specific market definition would collapse under scrutiny had an early, cheap chance to test it and declined. The pleaded market has therefore already survived the first practical stress point before trial.
The Facts
  • Filed July 13 by California, New York and 10 other states against the $111 billion acquisition. Two-week trial set for March 2027.
  • Three markets pleaded: film distribution for wide-release films, anticipated blockbuster film distribution, and cable TV.
  • Claimed concentration: nearly one-third of theatrical motion picture distribution; nearly one-third of basic cable channels, including 50 of the most popular cable channels.
  • Four distributors would control more than 90% of anticipated top-grossing films. Blockbusters account for 88% of box office revenue for films released over the past four years.
  • Statutory basis: the Clayton Act.
  • Bonta on remedies: the case "seeks to prevent the long-term structural impact from the loss of competition. An impact that can't be remedied with a few one-off, piecemeal promises."
  • Bonta on the framings he rejects: "It isn't about trusting that CBS News and CNN will remain independent and credible under one umbrella. It isn't about the future of streaming."
  • On the politics charge: "If it was, we would have been thrown out of court the day we filed." He notes the judge issued a temporary restraining order and that both companies agreed to pause the merger rather than contest preliminary injunction hearings.
  • Closing line: "And we intend to win."

Greenfield Tells Ellison the Only Settlement Left Is Selling a Whole Studio, Harry Potter and DC
The $7 million-a-day ticking fee starts October 1 and trial begins March 2. A WBD executive says a collapse leaves Larry Ellison out roughly $11 billion for nothing, against a company worth about $10 billion.
CEO Summary
LightShed's Rich Greenfield told investors this week that the merits of Paramount's antitrust defense no longer matter, because the trial calendar runs past the deal's June 4, 2027 termination date. To settle before the March 2 trial, he argues Paramount would have to buy Warner Bros. and then sell one of the two studios, its theatrical distribution, and major IP such as Harry Potter and all of DC Comics, plus potentially the combined cable networks including TNT, TBS and CNN. Puck's reporting adds the other side of the trade: a $7 billion break fee would cut WBD's net debt from about $30 billion to $23 billion and move it to investment grade.
Why This Matters
The shareholder detail is the leverage read. Most original WBD holders have exited and the register is now arbitrageurs, a base paid on resolution in either direction rather than on the combined company's future. That composition means WBD faces no owner pressure to help Paramount shrink the settlement price. Whatever scope of divestiture the states extract is funded entirely from Paramount's side of the ledger, and WBD's board is free to treat walking away as an acceptable outcome.
Specific Implication
Any deal tied to Harry Potter or DC IP rights should account for the possibility that ownership of that library changes hands as part of a structural remedy before the March 2027 trial.
The Facts
  • Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín set trial for March 2, running 12 days. Paramount had asked for a fall date to finish before the $7 million-a-day ticking fee starts October 1.
  • June 4, 2027 is the drop-dead date. On it, WBD can walk and collect $7 billion from Larry Ellison.
  • Greenfield: "While Paramount has repeatedly claimed that the state A.G.s and the W.G.A. have ignored reality to invent an antitrust case to block the merger... we believe it no longer matters."
  • Greenfield's proposed remedy: sell one of the two Hollywood studios, the theatrical distribution tied to it, and "several major" studio IP assets such as Harry Potter and all of DC Comics, enough to seed a new studio. Also raises divesting TNT, TBS and CNN.
  • He concedes the cost: Paramount "would lose a significant portion of the transaction synergies," though it keeps HBO and a bolstered library to combine with Paramount+ and Pluto TV. He cites Disney's sale of 50% of A&E Networks to Hearst at roughly 3.5x EBITDA as the discount risk on a forced linear sale.
  • Break-up math: $7 billion cuts WBD net debt from $30 billion to about $23 billion, leverage from 3.4x to 2.6x on roughly $8.7 billion of 2026 EBITDA, moving WBD to investment grade.
  • Zaslav forgoes the $31.75 all-cash consideration and a $550 million golden parachute in that scenario. Most original WBD shareholders have exited; the register is now arbitrageurs.
  • WBD Q2: revenue down 11% to $8.7 billion against $9.2 billion estimates; EBITDA $1.88 billion. Streaming and Studios revenue topped $3 billion for the first time, up 10%, EBITDA $512 million, up 60%. Wolfe Research's Peter Supino: "Studio flops in 2Q."
  • A WBD executive on a collapse: "a complete disaster for them... They have to settle with Bonta, but, you know, is he willing to settle?"
  • Both sides state intent to close. A WBD exec: "We want the $31.75. We want the deal to close." Zaslav on the Q2 call: "First and foremost, we're confident this transaction will close."
  • JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon on CNBC, August 5 (JPMorgan advises WBD and leads a $10 billion loan package to Paramount): state AGs intervening in mergers could damage "the future of American business." He added, "There may be examples of monopolistic behavior. But I have seen very little of that in my life."
  • Paramount chief legal officer Makan Delrahim on LinkedIn called for a federal-only merger review model like the EU's.
  • Disclosure carried in the piece: via a transaction, Zaslav is on the Puck cap table.

Spider-Man Is Now India's Biggest Hollywood Release Ever, in a Market Where Hollywood Held 8% Share This Year
Foreign films took 8% of the Indian market in the first half, down from 10% in 2025, while total Indian box office hit $661.66 million, the best first half since the pandemic. Sony has taken worldwide rights on "Ramayana: Part 1."
CEO Summary
"Spider-Man: Brand New Day" has become the highest-grossing Hollywood film of all time in India, reaching $52.8 million in 11 days and passing "Avatar: The Way of Water." It opened July 30, a day ahead of its global release, into a clear local calendar. India's overall first half was its strongest since the pandemic at $661.66 million, roughly 10% above 2025, but international films' share of that market fell to 8% from 10%.
Why This Matters
The shape of the Hollywood grosses carries the read. Below the record sits a steep drop to roughly $10 million results for "Obsession" and "Project Hail Mary." The record and the falling foreign share therefore describe the same market: one that clears a single Hollywood event at scale while the mid-tier import loses ground to local titles with a higher ceiling. Aggregate share is the wrong success metric for a studio in India; event scale and slot selection against the local calendar are the variables that moved.
Specific Implication
Territory bonuses or escalators tied to India performance should be benchmarked against the 8% foreign-film market share figure rather than the market's overall box office growth rate. Those are separate numbers, and only the former applies to a Hollywood release.
The Facts
  • "Spider-Man: Brand New Day": $52.8 million cume in India after a $10.6 million weekend, in 11 days. Passed "Avatar: The Way of Water" (2022) for the all-time Hollywood record.
  • Opened in India July 30, one day ahead of global release.
  • Foreign films typically hold 10-15% of the Indian market. In 2025 they took 10%, with "Avatar: Fire and Ash" the top Hollywood title at $26.4 million. The top local film, "Dhurandhar," took $104.8 million (Ormax Media).
  • In the first half of 2026, international films held 8%. "Obsession" grossed about $10 million, "Project Hail Mary" $9.2 million. "Dhurandhar: The Revenge" topped the half at $132 million.
  • India total box office, January to June 2026: $661.66 million (INR63.98 billion), the highest-grossing first half since the pandemic and about 10% above the first half of 2025 (Ormax Media).
  • "The Odyssey" (July 17) and "Obsession" (May 29) also cleared the INR1 billion ($10 million) benchmark in India this summer.
  • Upcoming: "Toxic" (Geetu Mohandas, starring Yash) August 26; "Ramayana: Part 1" expected for Diwali in November, recently picked up by Sony for worldwide distribution.
  • Globally, "Brand New Day" crossed $1 billion internationally in 12 days, second-fastest after "Avengers: Endgame," with $1.67 billion worldwide ($655 million domestic, $1.01 billion overseas). China led the international weekend at $29.1 million for a $186.7 million cume.

Roku's S-4 Shows 12 Buyers Were Approached and Only Fox Bid for the $22 Billion Platform
Roku's bankers approached 12 possible buyers for a platform in 100 million homes. Only Fox bid. Lachlan Murdoch told founder Anthony Wood he was coming in over a meeting in New York in April.
CEO Summary
An S-4 filed August 7 laid out how Fox Corp. came to buy Roku for $22 billion. Roku founder and CEO Anthony Wood raised succession with his board in September 2025, recommending a co-CEO and suggesting the board consider a sale; the board judged his exit the bigger risk and ran a market check instead. Advisors approached 12 counterparties and only Fox emerged as a serious bidder. Wood will stay roughly a year and take a Fox board seat; the deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 with $400 million in cost synergies.
Why This Matters
The projections in the filing carry the read. Fox underwrote Roku growing adjusted EBITDA from $650 million to $2.2 billion by 2030. That means the price was justified against the target's own forward case rather than forced by competitive tension, since no rival bid existed to force anything. A price set bilaterally on seller projections is the acquirer's conviction number. The same filing's record of a market check that produced no other serious interest stands as the market's counter-estimate of what the asset is worth to a buyer without Tubi to pair it with.
Specific Implication
A founder or CEO raising succession with the board, even as a limited proposal like a co-CEO recommendation, can prompt the board to initiate a sale process rather than the succession plan itself. Roku's own S-4 documents that sequence.
The Facts
  • S-4 filed August 7, 2026; the deal was announced in June 2026 at $22 billion.
  • September 26, 2025: Wood told the board he wanted to scale back, recommended a co-CEO, and said the board may want to consider a sale.
  • Board filing language: Wood stepping aside "posed potential risks to Roku's business, including... the loss of his expertise and strategic insights."
  • 12 counterparties approached, including Fox. Three others were deliberately not approached over "strategic business considerations" and commercial sensitivities; one, "Party K," was later included. Only Fox bid seriously.
  • Late April 2026, New York: Murdoch told Wood that Fox would bid, and asked about his perspectives on "artificial intelligence content and how to continue to drive revenue growth."
  • June 2026, New York: Murdoch raised a Fox board seat; Wood said he would consider a role "for only a limited period (likely one year)."
  • Roku reaches 100M+ households; Tubi has 110M users.
  • Fox projections: FY2026 revenue $16.9B, adjusted EBITDA $3.74B → 2031 revenue $21.5B, adjusted EBITDA $4.7B.
  • Roku projections: 2026 revenue $5.7B, adjusted EBITDA $650M → 2030 revenue $10.6B, adjusted EBITDA $2.2B.
  • Expected close H1 2027; $400M cost synergies.
  • Capitol Forum reported in August that the DOJ asked Fox and Roku to refile premerger notification forms for more review time.

Producers Say a Finished Series Sells 100% of the Time and a Pitch Sells 5%, and Private Equity Is Funding the Difference
Amplify's Joe Lewis, formerly head of originals at Amazon Studios, puts a pitch at a 5% chance of getting made, a pilot at 50-50, and a finished series at 100% in his company's experience. No streamer has a team that buys finished series.
CEO Summary
Former Amazon Studios original programming head Joe Lewis, now running Amplify Pictures with backing from private-markets investor Great Mountain Partners, told The Ankler that self-financing changes the odds at each stage: roughly 5 percent for a pitch, 50-50 for a pilot, and 100 percent for a completed series in his company's experience. Amplify has fully financed Mt. Mystic and The Earliest Show, both wrapped. Lewis says no streamer has a dedicated team for acquiring finished outside series, so every buy runs through an originals executive and a licensing executive together.
Why This Matters
The branding detail carries the structural read. Acquired shows are presented as originals, and "100 Foot Wave" runs as an HBO original, so the audience-facing product already treats a finished acquisition as interchangeable with a commission. What has not caught up is the buy side's org chart, and that gap is the actual arbitrage. A de-risked completed series is priced by executives whose mandates and budgets were built for pitches. That is why private capital can fund the difference and expect the spread to persist until a dedicated acquisitions desk closes it.
Specific Implication
Producers or creators with access to independent financing for a pilot or completed season have a documented path to a sale that does not depend on a streamer greenlighting a pitch. Lewis's stated pickup rates and the cited Gillis and Duplass outcomes are the record.

Spotify Is Testing a Podcast Ad-Skip Button for Paying Users, and Advertisers Are Not Pulling Spend
The skip button covers baked-in sponsorships creators sold themselves but does not apply to ads Spotify sells. Acast's CEO says about 10 percent of users actually skip, and no advertiser has pulled spend.
CEO Summary
Spotify began testing a "skip ahead" button last week for some paid subscribers, surfacing when they reach ads, promotions, intros, outros and baked-in sponsorships in podcasts. As Semafor first reported, the feature does not apply to ads Spotify sells itself. Oxford Advertising CEO Dan Granger says he has seen no advertiser pullback and expects minimal impact; Acast CEO Greg Glenday says some creators are unhappy and that Acast's own data shows roughly 10 percent of users skip, already priced into the ecosystem. Ads still register as delivered when skipped. Spotify says the test may or may not become a permanent feature.
Why This Matters
The design of the exemption carries the judgment. A skip control that spares only the platform's own inventory makes Spotify-sold placements the sole format guaranteed a listen. That operates as structural pressure on sponsors to route spend through Spotify's sales channel whether or not the test becomes permanent. Advertiser calm at the current skip rate does not change that direction; it only sets the pace.
Specific Implication
Podcast sponsorship deals structured around baked-in, creator-sold ad placements carry exposure to platform-side delivery changes that sit outside the creator's contract, as demonstrated by Spotify's unilateral rollout of this test.
The Facts
  • Spotify began rolling out the test last week for some paid subscribers; the "skip ahead" button surfaces at ads, promotions, intros, outros and baked-in sponsorships.
  • The feature does not apply to ads sold by Spotify itself. First reported by Semafor.
  • Ads are still technically delivered when skipped, so ad-delivery reporting is unchanged.
  • Dan Granger, CEO, Oxford Advertising: "Ad skipping is maybe scarier in theory than in practice, and so I don't think this is going to have major material direct impact on the brands that advertise." No advertiser pullback observed; most are taking a wait-and-see position.
  • Greg Glenday, CEO, Acast: some creators "are not happy about this and we will support them completely as they evaluate any recourse." Acast is working privately with Spotify on the rollout.
  • Acast internal metrics: about 10 percent of users choose to skip ads, already priced in.
  • Granger: the highest advertiser value is in host-read ads; excluding those from the skip while allowing other promos to be skipped would leave advertisers satisfied.
  • Spotify statement: "We regularly conduct tests at Spotify — some tests become permanent features, while others help inform future product development... We'll continue to evolve the experience as we learn."

Regal holds a written commitment for 30 films a year over three years with 45-day exclusive windows. Cinema United still opposes. The state AGs' trial starts March 2027.
CEO Summary
Paramount has offered theater chains contractually enforceable three-year commitments to release at least 30 films a year with 45-day exclusive theatrical windows and a 90-day hold before streaming, backed by financial penalties, and has offered to execute a consent decree to the state attorneys general to the same effect. Regal has such a written commitment per Deadline; AMC declined to comment, though both chains' CEOs have publicly backed the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Cinema United, the trade body representing the rest of exhibition, remains opposed, and the twelve state AGs' antitrust trial is set for March 2027.
Why This Matters
The Rentrak forward slates give the guarantee its actual bite. The combined companies show 35 films for 2027 but only 22 for 2028, so a penalty-backed 30-film floor would obligate Paramount to add releases in the first full post-merger year. That is precisely the point at which the Disney-Fox precedent shows merged studios cutting output. The commitment is costless in 2027 and binding in 2028, which is what separates it from a restatement of existing release plans.
Specific Implication
A theater chain has evidence that public support for the merger did not by itself secure a written, penalty-backed commitment from Paramount; only Regal has confirmed one on the record.

Baseline moviegoing has not rebuilt, which leaves the mid-budget wide release carrying the same theatrical risk it carried before the rebound.

A director with a large established platform audience, as demonstrated by Barker's and Parsons's combined $460.7 million domestic gross, has box office evidence to support pricing that audience into first-feature deal terms.

The platform selection is the tell. The video was withheld from the studio's official X, Threads, and TikTok accounts, the channels where criticism ultimately spread through reuploads. David Ellison lost the fight over the trial start date in the antitrust suit brought by state attorneys general and the WGA, and Deadline reports his $111 billion Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros. 'Spider-Man' Posts A $143 Million Second Weekend And Everything Else Gets Crushed

CEO Summary
Spider-Man: Brand New Day is tracking to a $143 million second weekend at 4,487 theaters, the third-best sophomore frame in domestic history and the first Sony title ever to clear $100 million in a second weekend. Its expected $653 million ten-day cume would be the highest in domestic box office history, ahead of Avengers: Endgame's $621.2 million. The instructive number is RelishMix's. "One Night Only" carried 355 million social impressions into release, more than triple the 99 million "Anyone But You" carried into a comparable opening. The film has grossed $23.5 million domestically since June 26 and $18 million across roughly 30 international territories.
Why This Matters
The misalignment Wilde is describing is structural. The premium is paid to the financier, but the cost of a skipped release falls on the filmmaker, whose next negotiation is priced partly on theatrical performance. On her account the correction ran on Ellison's goodwill, not on any contractual right, which is what made the outcome exceptional enough to recount from a festival stage. The film's seventh week in 342 theaters is the asset the declined premium purchased, and it accrues to the filmmaker's side of the ledger rather than to the financier who turned the money down.
Specific Implication
A director on an independently financed film has no guaranteed say over a theatrical-versus-streaming decision unless distribution-path approval is negotiated into the financing agreement.

Follows' line that "even a brilliant debut loses to an ordinary one with a better producer" carries the judgment the percentages do not state on their own. That makes the moment of entry, before any film exists to be judged, the point of maximum leverage in an emerging director's career.
Specific Implication
On a first-time director's project, the standing of the attached producer predicts the director's breakout odds more than the material does. Follows' data ties that attachment, not the debut's box office or reviews, to whether the director gets a second film within five years.

Net loss narrowed to $29 million from $107 million; television production revenue fell to $189 million on delivery timing.
Why This Matters
Feltheimer's unprompted endorsement of the Paramount-WBD merger, "uncertainty is the worst," is the frame to read the quarter through. A record film segment reported into an active consolidation cycle functions as sale-readiness evidence, and management is signaling comfort with that reading rather than resisting it. The quarter's job is less to prove the operating model than to establish the price a buyer would have to beat.
Specific Implication
Anyone benchmarking what Lionsgate itself retained from Michael should use the $105 million motion picture segment profit, not the $1.013 billion worldwide gross.
The Facts
  • Fiscal Q1 total revenue $777 million, up nearly 50 percent, ahead of Wall Street. Adjusted net income from continuing operations $18.9 million, or $0.06 per share. Net loss $29 million, narrowed from $107 million.
  • Motion picture revenue $587 million, more than double the prior year; segment profit $105 million, a Q1 record.
  • Television production revenue $189 million and profit $10.2 million, both down on episodic delivery timing. Scripted deliveries expected to double in fiscal 2028 from fiscal 2027.
  • Trailing 12-month library revenue $987 million.
  • Michael has grossed $1.013 billion worldwide and is the highest-grossing biopic ever.
  • Shares rose 2.4 percent to $13.26 in late trading, against a 52-week range from under $6 to near $17.
  • CEO Jon Feltheimer: "As we continue to execute our franchise strategy across a deep portfolio of branded intellectual properties, generate increased visibility and stability from our film and television library, and benefit from continued improvement in our operating environment, we are positioned to deliver strong growth in fiscal 2027 and beyond."
  • Brittany Snow recently joined Paul Feig's The Housemaid's Secret opposite Sydney Sweeney, Kirsten Dunst and Paul Anthony Kelly.
  • Feltheimer separately endorsed the Paramount-WBD merger, saying "uncertainty is the worst."

Microdrama Revenue Outside China Hits $3.6 Billion and ReelShort Turns Its First Profit
ReelShort went from $97 million of revenue in 2023 to a projected $1.05 billion this year, and Media Partners Asia expects the U.S. market alone to reach $3.7 billion by 2031.
CEO Summary
Media Partners Asia projects that ReelShort will generate $1.05 billion of revenue in 2026, up 34 percent, and post its first meaningful profit at scale, at roughly $40 million net. The firm sizes microdrama revenue outside China at $3.6 billion this year, up from $2.7 billion in 2025, reaching $9.5 billion by 2031 at a 21 percent compound annual growth rate. The margin story is marketing: user acquisition falls from just over half of revenue in 2025 to under 45 percent by 2028, with each percentage point worth about $10.5 million of EBITDA.
Why This Matters
The market-share table carries the structural point. Five apps hold about 79 percent of a category some 300 competitors are chasing, which means consolidation happened before most Western media companies took the format seriously. Entry at this stage means buying share or distribution, not launching an app. That narrows the realistic counterparties for any studio or platform seeking exposure to the category to the handful of incumbents already at scale.
Specific Implication
MPA's data ties ReelShort's improving margin to lower user-acquisition costs on franchise sequels rather than to increased content spending. Producers pitching successive installments in this format have a specific reported metric, declining per-title acquisition cost, to point to that is distinct from a general content-volume claim.
The Facts
  • ReelShort revenue: $97 million (2023), $400 million (2024), $785 million (2025), a projected $1.05 billion (2026). After an estimated $12 million net loss last year, MPA projects $63 million EBITDA and about $40 million net profit in 2026, rising to $306 million EBITDA at an 18 percent margin and $225 million net profit by 2028 on $1.7 billion of revenue.
  • Outside-China microdrama: $2.7 billion (2025), $3.6 billion (2026), $9.5 billion (2031), a 21 percent CAGR. U.S. from $1.5 billion to $3.7 billion; Asia Pacific ex-China tripling to $2.4 billion.
  • User acquisition and marketing: just over 50 percent of revenue in 2025 to under 45 percent by 2028; each point worth roughly $10.5 million of EBITDA.
  • Market share: ReelShort 29 percent, DramaBox 21 percent, DramaWave 13 percent, NetShort 10 percent, GoodShort 6 percent, remainder across roughly 300 smaller apps.
  • Asia contributes 12 percent of ReelShort revenue in 2026, rising to about $200 million and 14 percent in 2027. A Thailand AIS partnership has run since April; Indonesia and Philippines telco deals are expected by end of 2026; Japan and Korea production and distribution deals, including a Showbox co-production, launch in Q4.
  • MPA CEO Vivek Couto: "Microdrama has begun to be an earnings story rather than a growth story. ... What decides the next phase is distribution and unit economics, not necessarily content volume."
  • Lead analyst Myat Pan Phyu: "User acquisition is the swing factor. It falls from 55% of revenue in 2025 to 44% by 2028 on our model."
  • ReelShort was founded in 2022 by Crazy Maple Studio, has surpassed 286 million downloads and employs more than 1,600 staff plus freelance creators and production partners.

Apple passed on David E. Kelley's Bonfire of the Vanities after reading the pilot
Kelley already has two series at Apple, both renewed for second seasons, and the script still did not clear. A source on the pass: "Apple doesn't make that much, and the bar keeps getting higher."
CEO Summary
Apple TV has passed on a series adaptation of Tom Wolfe's "The Bonfire of the Vanities" from David E. Kelley and director Matt Reeves, in development since April, after executives read Kelley's pilot script. It would have been Kelley's third series at the streamer alongside "Margo's Got Money Troubles" and "Presumed Innocent," both renewed. The pass came inside a wider development-roster review that cut numerous scripts after head of development Matt Cherniss' U.S. team absorbed originals previously overseen by departed head of international Morgan Wandell. Kelley and Warner Bros. Television are shopping the project.
Why This Matters
The property's history sharpens what the shopping process will test. The 1990 film grossed under $16 million domestic on a $47 million budget, and a 2016 Amazon limited series never advanced. The package's market value therefore rests entirely on the Kelley-Reeves auspices overcoming an IP track record that argues against the material. Buyers reading that same history will price the auspices, not the title, which makes this a live test of how much a top-tier package is worth detached from IP heat.
Specific Implication
A showrunner with renewed series already running at a curated-slate buyer should not treat that history as a guarantee that a new pilot clears. Kelley and Warner Bros. Television moved directly to shopping Bonfire elsewhere rather than continuing to negotiate with Apple.
The Facts
  • In development at Apple TV since April; written by Kelley, directed by Matt Reeves; produced by Warner Bros. Television.
  • Executives were unimpressed with the pilot script, per multiple sources. Would have been Kelley's third Apple series after "Margo's Got Money Troubles" and "Presumed Innocent," both renewed for season two.
  • Kelley and WBTV are actively shopping the project elsewhere.
  • Pass followed a slate review in which Cherniss' U.S. team absorbed originals previously run by Wandell, who departed in May.
  • Source quote: "Everybody loves David; nothing about it was easy. Apple doesn't make that much, and the bar keeps getting higher."
  • Prior attempts: Warners' 1990 film, $47 million budget, under $16 million domestic; a 2016 Amazon limited series from Chuck Lorre and Warners that never advanced.
  • Reps for Apple and David E. Kelley Productions declined comment.

Paramount pushed its WBD debt exchange deadline for the seventh time since June
Seven extensions since June 12, now to Aug. 21. As of Aug. 6, 65.43% of the tender notes and 76.04% of the exchange notes were tendered, and holders can still withdraw at any time.
CEO Summary
Paramount Skydance extended the expiration dates on its cash tender offers and note exchange offers for Warner Bros. Discovery debt to Aug. 21, 2026, the seventh such extension since June 12. The offers cover notes issued by Discovery Global Holdings and Discovery Communications, and Paramount says it expects to keep extending until settlement can occur on or promptly after the acquisition closes. As of Aug. 6, roughly 65.43% of tender offer notes and 76.04% of exchange offer notes had been validly tendered, figures Paramount says are not representative of final results.
Why This Matters
The regulatory sequence gives the extensions their meaning. The UK CMA approved the acquisition on Aug. 6 and settlement is anticipated in Q3, so the rolling extensions now function as a closing countdown rather than a sign of trouble. An extension pattern that outlives the last major regulatory gate implies Paramount is holding the offers open for settlement mechanics, not approvals, which shifts the remaining execution risk from regulators to the closing timetable itself.
Specific Implication
A counterparty with a deal or negotiation tied to the timing of the Paramount-WBD acquisition closing should track the tender/exchange offer extension notices as a more current public signal than earnings-call commentary. The company says the notices will keep rolling until settlement is near closing.
The Facts

  • Issuers: Discovery Global Holdings, Inc. (formerly WarnerMedia Holdings, Inc.) and Discovery Communications, LLC. Cash for tender notes; newly issued Paramount notes for exchange notes.
  • Tendered as of 5:00 p.m. Aug. 6: approximately 65.43% of tender offer notes, 76.04% of exchange offer notes. Paramount does not view these as representative of final results.
  • Withdrawal permitted at any time prior to the expiration date. Settlement anticipated in Q3 2026.

Disney's trading card revenue has quadrupled since 2023
Disney licensing will move about $63 billion in product this year, the most of any company License Global tracks, and the fastest-growing piece of it is cards. Consumer Products moves into the Entertainment division later this year.
CEO Summary
Disney executives told The Hollywood Reporter that the company's trading card revenue has quadrupled since 2023, inside a category some analysts size at $50 billion annually. Disney runs the business through licensees: Topps for Topps Chrome Disney, Topps Chrome Marvel and Star Wars Masterworks, Ravensburger for Disney Lorcana, and Hasbro for Marvel and Spider-Man editions of Magic: The Gathering. Later this year Disney Consumer Products leaves the Experiences division and joins Entertainment, and DCP already engages the studios early so new characters can be built into card products.
Why This Matters
The gap to the field is the structural fact. Authentic Brands Group, the second-largest licensor License Global tracks, moves $36 billion in product, leaving Disney's licensing operation at nearly twice the scale of its closest comparable. In a category that runs independent of any release calendar, that advantage compounds in weak slate years as readily as strong ones. That is the logic of moving consumer products inside the division that decides what gets made: collectible extensibility becomes an input to greenlight decisions rather than a downstream royalty stream.
Specific Implication
For talent or rights holders negotiating a new franchise project, autograph and screen-used-material reservations are a term worth raising at the character-development stage rather than after release. Disney Consumer Products is moving into the Entertainment division and states it engages studios before a title's characters are finalized.
The Facts
  • Disney trading card revenue has quadrupled since 2023. Analysts size the overall market at roughly $50 billion annually.
  • Disney products will generate about $63 billion in sales this year per License Global, the most of any company tracked; Authentic Brands Group is second at $36 billion.
  • Partners: Topps (Topps Chrome Disney, Topps Chrome Marvel, Star Wars Masterworks), Ravensburger (Disney Lorcana), Hasbro (Marvel and Spider-Man Magic: The Gathering).
  • Disney Consumer Products moves from Experiences into Entertainment later this year.
  • David Leiner, president of Trading Cards for Topps: "they're not just entertainment brands, they're multi-generational storytelling engines."
  • Ryan Reynolds bought a Hugh Jackman-signed Wolverine card at Fanatics Fest last month for $800 plus a doodled Dogpool card, down from a $1,000 ask.

Netflix and MLB are developing a Yankees anthology built like The Crown
Josh Wakely secured the rights from MLB before setting the project, and MLB Studios is producing rather than licensing. Netflix already streams MLB opening night, the Home Run Derby, and Field of Dreams on Aug. 13.
CEO Summary
Netflix is developing an untitled scripted drama about the New York Yankees with MLB Studios, Jason Bateman's Aggregate Films, and writer/director/producer Josh Wakely, who secured the underlying rights from MLB and developed the concept. The Ankler reports the plan is an anthology in the mold of "The Crown," each season covering a different Yankees superstar; no writer is attached and no first-season subject is set. The project sits alongside Netflix's expanded 2026 to 2028 MLB live package.
Why This Matters
The credit block carries the structural point. Nine executive producers spanning the league, Aggregate, Brillstein Entertainment Partners and outside financiers were locked at setup, before any creative element defined the show. The project's economics were divided at the rights layer first. A writer boarding now enters a structure whose upside was allocated before the creative work began, the inverse of the development order in which material attracts the package.
Specific Implication
A rights holder sitting on a deep archive with an active live-rights deal at the same platform can point to MLB's arrangement as precedent for negotiating a producing credit and financial stake in scripted development rather than a flat license fee. MLB produces through MLB Studios rather than licensing its name.
The Facts

  • Anthology structure akin to "The Crown," one superstar per season, per The Ankler. No writer attached; first-season subject undetermined.

Chinese AI Models Are Still Generating 'The Office' Clips While Three Studios Sue
MiniMax withheld Hailuo 3 from the U.S. over the pending Disney, Universal and Warner Bros. suit, and a U.S. venture investor generated a Dwight-and-Jim clip through an aggregator on MiniMax's own servers.
CEO Summary
MiniMax released Hailuo 3 this week without direct availability in the U.S. or European Union, citing "ongoing copyright-related legal proceedings specifically concerning generative video AI." Andreessen Horowitz partner Justine Moore then generated a recognizable clip of Dwight and Jim from The Office using a simple H3 prompt through Krea, an aggregator, with the prompt routing back through MiniMax's servers. Separately, the startup VN.ai produced bootleg images of Elsa, Shrek and Buzz Lightyear through ByteDance's Seedream 5.0 via a third-party API.
Why This Matters
The ByteDance comparison isolates what actually changes model behavior. Guardrails arrived at Seedance only after cease-and-desist letters followed the Tom Cruise-Brad Pitt deepfake. MiniMax, facing litigation rather than a commercial relationship it needs to protect, responded by restricting distribution and leaving the model itself unchanged. Enforcement pressure produces model-level restraint only where the developer has U.S. market exposure at stake; where it does not, legal action redraws distribution maps without touching outputs.
Specific Implication
Rights holders negotiating AI licensing or enforcement terms with a model provider should require that restrictions bind third-party aggregators and API resellers directly, not only the provider's own first-party product. MiniMax's withholding of Hailuo 3 from the U.S. did not prevent a recognizable clip from being generated through the aggregator Krea on MiniMax's own servers.
The Facts
  • MiniMax released Hailuo 3 (H3) this week; it is not directly available in the U.S. or EU but has gone viral outside China through third-party access.
  • Justine Moore, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, generated a clip of Dwight and Jim from The Office with a simple H3 text prompt in Krea. The prompt routed through MiniMax's servers.
  • Disney, Universal and Warner Bros. allege in their suit that Hailuo "pirates and plunders copyrighted works on a massive scale," citing MiniMax's own YouTube promotion using Deadpool, Wolverine and The Joker videos. Those videos have been removed. MiniMax denies the allegations and did not respond to a request for comment.
  • At launch, a MiniMax representative said the full model would not be available in the U.S. because of "ongoing copyright-related legal proceedings specifically concerning generative video AI."
  • ByteDance released Seedance 2.5 the same week without comparable IP reproduction. Seedance 2.0 had produced the viral Tom Cruise versus Brad Pitt deepfake, drawing cease-and-desist letters from Netflix, Disney and others.
  • VN.ai generated bootleg images of Elsa, Shrek and Buzz Lightyear through Seedream 5.0 via a third-party API, per research reports seen by Deadline. Character prompts were often denied; specifying exact pixel sizes produced a recognizable Buzz Lightyear.
  • ByteDance statement: "ByteDance launches models with safeguards designed to prevent unauthorized use of intellectual property, and continually works to expand and strengthen these in collaboration with rightsholders and creative communities."
  • U.S. studios and the Motion Picture Association were approached for comment.

Versant Raised Guidance in Its Second Quarter as a Standalone Cable Company
Advertising revenue fell just under 1 percent, against a 13 percent drop in the same quarter a year earlier, and the company raised full-year guidance to as much as $6.45 billion.
CEO Summary
Versant, the cable-focused NBCUniversal spinoff running CNBC, MS NOW, USA and Golf Channel, reported June-quarter revenue of $1.64 billion, down 3.8 percent. Linear distribution fell 6.3 percent to $954 million while platforms revenue excluding the divested SportsEngine rose 9.3 percent to $225 million, which the CFO called the fastest-growing part of the group. Net income fell 30 percent to $211 million on separation costs, and adjusted EBITDA fell 9 percent to $624 million, but the company raised full-year 2026 guidance to $6.2 billion to $6.45 billion of revenue and $1.9 billion to $2.05 billion of adjusted EBITDA.
Why This Matters
The news ratings are the leverage story inside the quarter. MS NOW posted a seventh consecutive month of audience growth and CNBC delivered its best quarter in more than five years. That hands Versant a programming argument in carriage renewals at precisely the moment eroding distribution revenue would otherwise strip its negotiating position. The company is rebuilding leverage through audience performance and owned AVOD brands rather than defending bundle economics, the behavior of a builder rather than a harvest vehicle.
Specific Implication
A rights holder negotiating a mid-tier live sports package with Versant specifically should expect a dual-window structure, premium pay-TV carriage on USA paired with a free AVOD tier, built into the same deal. That expectation is based on the terms Lazarus described for the Bundesliga acquisition.
The Facts
  • Q2 revenue $1.64 billion, down 3.8 percent from $1.7 billion.
  • Linear distribution down 6.3 percent to $954 million. Advertising $423 million, down just under 1 percent, against a 13 percent decline in the year-earlier quarter. Content licensing unchanged at $43 million.
  • Platforms revenue up 0.8 percent to $212 million; excluding SportsEngine, up 9.3 percent to $225 million. CFO and COO Anand Kini called platforms the "fastest growing part" of the group, citing Fandango and GolfNow.
  • Net income attributable to Versant down 30 percent to $211 million on lower revenue and one-time separation costs including higher tax expenses after the SportsEngine divestiture. Adjusted EBITDA down 9 percent to $624 million.
  • Full-year 2026 guidance raised: revenue $6.2 billion to $6.45 billion, adjusted EBITDA $1.9 billion to $2.05 billion.
  • Lazarus: "AVOD is one of the fastest growing areas in media, and we enjoy clear advantages from the well known Fandango brand: broad, connected TV distribution, rich first-party data and unique and exclusive content."
  • On Bundesliga: "a significant number of hours — 600 or 700 hours of live sports — and be able to both serve our pay TV customers with premium matches on USA and create a new marketplace for ourselves in free AVOD."
  • MS NOW posted a seventh consecutive month of year-over-year audience growth and was the No. 1 news organization on YouTube in June. CNBC delivered its highest-rated quarter in more than five years.

Movies and Music Added 9,900 Jobs in July While the U.S. Economy Lost 23,000
Broadcasting and content providers shed 1,500 jobs in the same month, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics revised 103,000 jobs out of its May and June estimates.
CEO Summary
The U.S. economy lost 23,000 jobs in July against analyst estimates of a gain as large as 100,000, and the Bureau of Labor Statistics revised prior months down by a combined 103,000. Employment in movies and music rose by 9,900 to 332,700, reversing some earlier declines, while broadcasting and content providers fell by 1,500 to 335,800. Unemployment edged down to 4.1 percent, a figure the report attributes partly to people leaving the labor force.
Why This Matters
Zandi's characterization of job growth as "at a virtual standstill, and concentrated in a few sectors" places the entertainment number in its real context. Production hiring is running counter-cyclically, driven by content-spend and production-calendar timing rather than macro conditions. The sector's employment cycle is on its own clock, which means a weakening national labor market is not the read-through for production headcount, in either direction.
Specific Implication
Below-the-line crew negotiating current rates should note that July's hiring gain in movies and music employment came alongside wage growth of 3.2 percent year over year, below the inflation pace economists in the report describe. Added headcount has not been accompanied by comparable pay growth.
The Facts
  • U.S. economy lost 23,000 jobs in July. Analysts had estimated a gain of as much as 100,000.
  • Movies and music employment rose 9,900 to 332,700. Broadcasting and content providers fell 1,500 to 335,800.
  • Unemployment fell slightly to 4.1 percent, affected by labor-force exits.
  • Declines in local government education and retail trade. Health care added 22,000 positions, at a slower pace than previous months.
  • May and June estimates revised down by a combined 103,000.
  • Average hourly earnings changed by two cents to $37.62, up 3.2 percent year over year.
  • Heather Long, chief economist, Navy Federal: "The Fed's job just got a lot harder. The labor market is stalling again. Many industries shedding jobs or flat."
  • Mark Zandi, chief economist, Moody's Analytics: "There's no sugar coating the overarching message in the July jobs report – the economy is struggling." Job growth is "at a virtual standstill, and concentrated in a few sectors."

Roku gave a 24/7 FAST channel to an AI startup that produced none of it itself
Fairground launched in 2025, did not make the programming itself, and is developing AI-generated Robin Hood and Dracula adaptations. Roku carried it alongside three catalog channels the same week.
CEO Summary
Roku added four channels this week: catalog feeds for "Mad TV," "Whose Line Is It Anyway?" and Black sitcoms, plus Fairground AI Creator TV, a 24/7 stream of entirely AI-generated content from Colin Petrie-Norris' startup Fairground. The programming comes from creators partnered with Fairground rather than from Fairground itself, and has no consistent theme or genre. Fairground launched in 2025 and is reportedly developing AI-generated adaptations of Robin Hood and Dracula.
Why This Matters
The Verge's own verdict, that Roku "hasn't really gotten all that much out of the deal," points at the actual trade. Carriage was granted for positioning value, not programming value, at a shelf-space cost of effectively zero. Once a platform will pay out distribution for a generative-AI claim, conventionally produced programming is competing not only with cheaper content but with suppliers whose entire contribution is an aggregation arrangement. Those suppliers commit no production capital of their own.
Specific Implication
Rights holders considering AI licensing terms with distributors like Roku should note that Fairground's reported next projects, Robin Hood and Dracula, are both public domain. Its channel and its adaptation pipeline can scale without generating licensing revenue for any rights holder.
The Facts
  • Four new Roku channels this week: "Mad TV," "Whose Line Is It Anyway?," a Black sitcoms feed, and Fairground AI Creator TV.
  • Fairground AI Creator TV is a 24/7 stream of entirely AI-generated content. Founded by Colin Petrie-Norris; the startup launched in 2025.
  • Programming is made by content creators partnered with Fairground, not by Fairground; no consistent theme or genre.
  • Fairground is reportedly working on AI-generated adaptations of Robin Hood and Dracula.
  • Viewers can scrub only a few seconds forward or back and cannot select titles, as with any FAST channel.
  • The Verge, after about an hour of viewing, described the output as "the same kind of short-form slop that text-to-video models have become known for" and said Roku "hasn't really gotten all that much out of the deal aside from the ability to say that it's getting in on the gen AI craze."
